Normalized Deviation Faithfulness (NDF) is a more robust evaluation metric for query circuits compared to Normalized Faithfulness Score (NFS).
Query circuits enable local, prompt-level explanations of LLM decisions, offering a step towards scalable interpretability.
papers.limitation:
The method neglects combinatorial interactions among edges, which is a fundamental limitation of using indirect effects as edge scores.
The work focuses on queries with single-token outputs (e.g., option IDs) and does not address multi-token generations.
There is no automated method for interpreting the functionalities of identified edges and nodes; manual investigation is not scalable.
future_direction: Develop methods to account for combinatorial interactions among edges in circuit discovery.
Extend query circuit discovery to multi-token generations.
Integrate automated interpretability methods to explain the functionalities of discovered circuits.
papers.abstract: Explaining why a language model produces a particular output requires local, input-level explanations. Existing methods uncover global capability circuits (e.g., indirect object identification), but not why the model answers a specific input query in a particular way. We introduce query circuits, which directly trace the information flow inside a model that maps a specific input to the output. Unlike surrogate-based approaches (e.g., sparse autoencoders), query circuits are identified within the model itself, resulting in more faithful and computationally accessible explanations. To make query circuits practical, we address two challenges. First, we introduce Normalized Deviation Faithfulness (NDF), a robust metric to evaluate how well a discovered circuit recovers the model's decision for a specific input, and is broadly applicable to circuit discovery beyond our setting. Second, we develop sampling-based methods to efficiently identify circuits that are sparse yet faithfully describe the model's behavior. Across benchmarks (IOI, arithmetic, MMLU, and ARC), we find that there exist extremely sparse query circuits within the model that can recover much of its performance on single queries. For example, a circuit covering only 1.3% of model connections can recover about 60% of performance on an MMLU questions. Overall, query circuits provide a step towards faithful, scalable explanations of how language models process individual inputs.

papers.title: Uncovering Latent Chain of Thought Vectors in Language Models
papers.research_question: Can steering vectors derived from LM activations induce Chain-of-Thought reasoning without natural language prompting?
papers.core_contribution: Steering vectors derived from contrastive activations can induce Chain-of-Thought reasoning in frozen language models, matching or exceeding the performance of traditional CoT prompting.
papers.conclusion: Steering vector injection can effectively induce Chain-of-Thought reasoning in language models without prompting, suggesting reasoning capabilities are encoded in activation and weight space. The method matches or exceeds CoT prompting performance, with injection timing influencing results.
papers.key_findings:
Steering vector injection induces CoT reasoning without natural language prompts.
The method achieves competitive or superior performance compared to CoT prompting on GSM8k, MMLU, ARC AI2, and AGI Eval benchmarks.
The approach generalizes to unseen data, as shown on the SAT Math section of AGI Eval.
Different injection strategies (single vs. continuous) yield varying performance across benchmarks.
Steered models produce more structured, step-by-step reasoning outputs while retaining natural language fluency.
papers.limitation: Performance varies with injection strategy and may not be optimized.
future_direction: Explore different methods for injecting steering vectors to optimize performance and reliability
Investigate generalization capabilities of steering vectors across different models
Scale up the approach to larger models
papers.abstract: In this work, we examine how targeted perturbations in the activation space of Language Models (LMs) can encode complex reasoning patterns. We inject steering vectors, derived from LM activations, into LMs during inference time and study whether these vectors can induce Chain-of-Thought (CoT) reasoning in LMs without the need for natural language prompting. We demonstrate this approach on Llama3 8B Instruct and Mistral 7B v0.2 Instruct and show that activation-space interventions achieve competitive, if not superior, performance compared to traditional CoT prompting across multiple reasoning benchmarks, including GSM8k, MMLU, AGI Eval, and ARC AI2. These findings suggest that neural network activations can encode reasoning patterns, offering a new application of activation space manipulation as a tool for tuning model behavior.

papers.title: Compositional Generalization in Grounded Language Learning via Induced Model Sparsity
papers.research_question: How can induced model sparsity help achieve compositional generalization and sample efficiency in grounded language learning?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces a Sparse Factored Attention model that leverages sparsity and factor compositionality to achieve compositional generalization and sample efficiency in grounded language learning for navigation tasks.
papers.conclusion: The paper concludes that induced sparsity and factor compositionality enable compositional generalization and sample efficiency in grounded language learning, as demonstrated by the Sparse Factored Attention model.
papers.key_findings:
Sparse Factored Attention achieves high performance on both in-distribution and out-of-distribution goals with few samples.
The model learns correct correspondences between words and attributes, as shown by visualization of embedding correlations.
Standard architectures (Transformer, FiLM) fail to generalize compositionally or require large amounts of data.
The proposed training method with a discriminator enables learning goal identification without labels.
The decoupled architecture (goal identification + planning) improves sample efficiency.
papers.limitation:
The goal identification and planning methods do not work over compound goals.
The discriminator training method requires that the dataset can be partitioned into subsets corresponding to each goal.
Measuring sample efficiency is not well-specified because each training step could improve the model arbitrarily.
The environment assumptions are strong: fully observable state space, knowledge of connectivity, and disentangled factors.
papers.abstract: We provide a study of how induced model sparsity can help achieve compositional generalization and better sample efficiency in grounded language learning problems. We consider simple language-conditioned navigation problems in a grid world environment with disentangled observations. We show that standard neural architectures do not always yield compositional generalization. To address this, we design an agent that contains a goal identification module that encourages sparse correlations between words in the instruction and attributes of objects, composing them together to find the goal. The output of the goal identification module is the input to a value iteration network planner. Our agent maintains a high level of performance on goals containing novel combinations of properties even when learning from a handful of demonstrations. We examine the internal representations of our agent and find the correct correspondences between words in its dictionary and attributes in the environment.

papers.title: Improving Neuron-level Interpretability with White-box Language Models
papers.research_question: Can building sparsity directly into the language model architecture (via a white-box design) improve neuron-level interpretability compared to post-hoc methods like sparse autoencoders?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces a white-box transformer-like architecture (crate) that embeds sparse coding directly into the model, leading to significantly improved neuron-level interpretability compared to standard transformers like GPT-2.
papers.conclusion: Replacing the standard transformer architecture with the white-box crate model significantly improves neuron-level interpretability, pointing towards a promising direction for building more interpretable foundation models with built-in sparse coding.
papers.key_findings:
crate achieves up to 103% relative improvement in neuron-level interpretability over GPT-2 across multiple evaluation metrics.
The improved interpretability is steady across different layers and model sizes.
crate's interpretability stems from its ability to consistently and distinctively activate on relevant tokens.
crate has more optimal representations for interpretability than GPT-2, as applying sparse autoencoders (SAE) to crate yields smaller improvements than applying SAE to GPT-2.
crate can be steered without the reconstruction loss inherent in post-hoc SAE methods.
papers.limitation: The performance of crate on the next-token prediction task is not as good as GPT-2, potentially due to the introduction of sparsity.
future_direction: Investigate a better trade-off between performance and interpretability in language models with built-in sparsity.
Research more qualitative mechanisms in white-box language models and how to use them for downstream edits.
papers.abstract: Neurons in auto-regressive language models like GPT-2 can be interpreted by analyzing their activation patterns. Recent studies have shown that techniques such as dictionary learning, a form of post-hoc sparse coding, enhance this neuron-level interpretability. In our research, we are driven by the goal to fundamentally improve neural network interpretability by embedding sparse coding directly within the model architecture, rather than applying it as an afterthought. In our study, we introduce a white-box transformer-like architecture named Coding RAte TransformEr (CRATE), explicitly engineered to capture sparse, low-dimensional structures within data distributions. Our comprehensive experiments showcase significant improvements (up to 103% relative improvement) in neuron-level interpretability across a variety of evaluation metrics. Detailed investigations confirm that this enhanced interpretability is steady across different layers irrespective of the model size, underlining CRATE's robust performance in enhancing neural network interpretability. Further analysis shows that CRATE's increased interpretability comes from its enhanced ability to consistently and distinctively activate on relevant tokens. These findings point towards a promising direction for creating white-box foundation models that excel in neuron-level interpretation.

papers.title: Does higher interpretability imply better utility? A Pairwise Analysis on Sparse Autoencoders
papers.research_question: Does higher interpretability of Sparse Autoencoder (SAE) features imply better steering utility for large language models?
papers.core_contribution: The paper finds only a weak positive association between SAE feature interpretability and steering utility, and introduces a new feature selection criterion (∆Token Confidence) that significantly improves steering performance.
papers.conclusion: There is a significant divergence between SAE interpretability and steering utility, suggesting that prioritizing interpretability does not guarantee improved steering performance.
papers.key_findings:
Interpretability shows a relatively weak positive association with steering utility (Kendall's τb ≈ 0.298).
∆Token Confidence effectively selects features with strong steering performance, improving steering score by 52.52% over the previous best method.
After selecting high-utility features with ∆Token Confidence, the correlation between interpretability and utility vanishes or becomes negative.
future_direction: Developing advanced post-training feature selection protocols or fundamentally new, utility-oriented SAE training paradigms.
papers.abstract: Sparse Autoencoders (SAEs) are widely used to steer large language models (LLMs), based on the assumption that their interpretable features naturally enable effective model behavior steering. Yet, a fundamental question remains unanswered: does higher interpretability indeed imply better steering utility? To answer this question, we train 90 SAEs across three LLMs (Gemma-2-2B, Qwen-2.5-3B, Gemma-2-9B), spanning five architectures and six sparsity levels, and evaluate their interpretability and steering utility based on SAEBench (arXiv:2501.12345) and AxBench (arXiv:2502.23456) respectively, and perform a rank-agreement analysis via Kendall's rank coefficients (tau b). Our analysis reveals only a relatively weak positive association (tau b approx 0.298), indicating that interpretability is an insufficient proxy for steering performance. We conjecture the interpretability utility gap may stem from the selection of SAE features, as not all of them are equally effective for steering. To further find features that truly steer the behavior of LLMs, we propose a novel selection criterion called Delta Token Confidence, which measures how much amplifying a feature changes the next token distribution. We show that our method improves the steering performance of three LLMs by 52.52 percent compared to the current best output score based criterion (arXiv:2503.34567). Strikingly, after selecting features with high Delta Token Confidence, the correlation between interpretability and utility vanishes (tau b approx 0), and can even become negative. This further highlights the divergence between interpretability and utility for the most effective steering features.

papers.title: Correctness-Optimized Residual Activation Lens (CORAL): Transferrable and Calibration-Aware Inference-Time Steering
papers.research_question: How can we improve both accuracy and calibration of LLMs during inference by directly steering using correctness signals from internal activations, rather than optimizing proxies?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces CORAL, a lightweight inference-time steering method that uses regularized MLP probes on residual activations to improve accuracy and calibration in MCQA tasks, with demonstrated transferability across benchmarks.
papers.conclusion: CORAL provides a compute-efficient, transferable, and calibration-aware approach to improve MCQA performance during inference by extracting distributed correctness signals via regularized probes.
papers.key_findings:
CORAL consistently improves accuracy and calibration across three 7B models and multiple MCQA benchmarks.
CORAL's learned steering directions transfer without retraining to four held-out benchmarks, averaging 14% accuracy and 49% ECE improvements.
Correctness signals are distributed across many neurons and require supervised aggregation; sparse methods like SAE fail to capture them.
Middle layers (17-21) contain the most useful correctness signals for steering.
Regularized probes capture distributed correctness signals that sparse methods miss.
papers.limitation:
Limited to multiple-choice question answering; generalization to free-form generation is open.
Requires labeled data to train probes, which may not be available for all domains or languages.
Adds inference latency due to activation extraction and probe prediction.
Transfer performance depends on similarity between source and target tasks; dissimilar tasks yield smaller improvements.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) exhibit persistent miscalibration, especially after instruction tuning and preference alignment. Modified training objectives can improve calibration, but retraining is expensive. Inference-time steering offers a lightweight alternative, yet most existing methods optimize proxies for correctness rather than correctness itself. We introduce CORAL (Correctness-Optimized Residual Activation Lens), a regularized inference-time steering method that captures distributed correctness signals from model internal activations using weight-decay MLP probes. We evaluate CORAL across three 7B-parameter models and find that it consistently improves accuracy by 10\% and expected calibration error (ECE) by 50\% on average. We additionally demonstrate that these gains transfer without retraining to the complete published test sets of four held-out benchmarks (ARC-Challenge, HellaSwag, Math-MC, OpenBookQA), averaging 14\% accuracy improvements and 49\% ECE improvements. Our results support the hypothesis that distributed information in model internals can be extracted using regularized probes when individual neurons are insufficient. CORAL thus provides a compute-efficient, transferable, and calibration-aware approach to improve MCQA performance during inference.

papers.title: Endogenous Resistance to Activation Steering in Language Models
papers.research_question: This paper investigates whether large language models can monitor their own internal states and resist task-misaligned activation steering during inference, a phenomenon termed Endogenous Steering Resistance (ESR).
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces and characterizes Endogenous Steering Resistance (ESR), showing that large language models can self-correct during inference when subjected to task-misaligned activation steering, and provides causal evidence for internal consistency-checking circuits.
papers.conclusion: ESR demonstrates that large language models have internal self-monitoring mechanisms that can resist activation steering, which has implications for both robustness and safety, highlighting the need to understand and control these mechanisms.
papers.key_findings:
Llama-3.3-70B exhibits substantial Endogenous Steering Resistance (ESR), while smaller models from the Llama-3 and Gemma-2 families show it less frequently.
26 SAE latents are identified as off-topic detectors and causally linked to ESR; ablating them reduces the multi-attempt rate by 25%.
ESR can be enhanced through meta-prompts, increasing the multi-attempt rate by 4.3× for Llama-3.3-70B.
Fine-tuning on self-correction examples can induce ESR-like behavior in smaller models, but only increases attempt frequency without improving success rate.
ESR has dual implications: it could protect against adversarial manipulation but might interfere with beneficial safety interventions.
papers.limitation:
Reliance on single-layer SAEs limits tracing of inter-layer dynamics.
Only 5 models tested, making it difficult to disentangle effects of scale, architecture, and training.
Judge-based evaluation involves subjective assessment of response quality.
future_direction: Investigate whether ESR emerges from RLHF or exists in pretrained representations.
Study how ESR responds to safety-relevant steering.
Explore whether ESR can be adversarially circumvented.
papers.abstract: Large language models can resist task-misaligned activation steering during inference, sometimes recovering mid-generation to produce improved responses even when steering remains active. We term this Endogenous Steering Resistance (ESR). Using sparse autoencoder (SAE) latents to steer model activations, we find that Llama-3.3-70B shows substantial ESR, while smaller models from the Llama-3 and Gemma-2 families exhibit the phenomenon less frequently. We identify 26 SAE latents that activate differentially during off-topic content and are causally linked to ESR in Llama-3.3-70B. Zero-ablating these latents reduces the multi-attempt rate by 25%, providing causal evidence for dedicated internal consistency-checking circuits. We demonstrate that ESR can be deliberately enhanced through both prompting and training: meta-prompts instructing the model to self-monitor increase the multi-attempt rate by 4x for Llama-3.3-70B, and fine-tuning on self-correction examples successfully induces ESR-like behavior in smaller models. These findings have dual implications: ESR could protect against adversarial manipulation but might also interfere with beneficial safety interventions that rely on activation steering. Understanding and controlling these resistance mechanisms is important for developing transparent and controllable AI systems. Code is available at github.com/agencyenterprise/endogenous-steering-resistance.

papers.title: LLM Circuit Analyses Are Consistent Across Training and Scale
papers.research_question: Do circuit analyses of LLMs generalize across training time and model scale?
papers.core_contribution: Circuit analyses are consistent across training and scale: task abilities and supporting functional components emerge at similar token counts across model sizes, and the overarching algorithms implemented by circuits remain stable even when individual components change.
papers.conclusion: Circuit analyses generalize well over both training and scale, suggesting that studies on small models at the end of pre-training can inform understanding of larger models and models with longer training.
papers.key_findings:
Task abilities and functional components (e.g., induction heads, name-mover heads) emerge consistently at similar token counts across different model scales.
The algorithm implemented by a circuit remains stable over training even when the specific attention heads implementing it change.
Circuit size correlates with model size and can fluctuate over time while the algorithm remains the same.
Components like induction heads emerge around 2B tokens across scales, paralleling task learning curves.
Circuit analyses conducted on small models at the end of pre-training provide insights that generalize to larger models and longer training runs.
papers.limitation:
The study does not include fine-tuning or other post-training techniques.
Circuit completeness is challenging to verify.
The findings need validation on more complex circuits and those based on SAE latents.
future_direction: Validation on more complex circuits and those based on SAE latents.
Investigating the load-balancing mechanism that maintains task performance when components change.
papers.abstract: Most currently deployed large language models (LLMs) undergo continuous training or additional finetuning. By contrast, most research into LLMs' internal mechanisms focuses on models at one snapshot in time (the end of pre-training), raising the question of whether their results generalize to real-world settings. Existing studies of mechanisms over time focus on encoder-only or toy models, which differ significantly from most deployed models. In this study, we track how model mechanisms, operationalized as circuits, emerge and evolve across 300 billion tokens of training in decoder-only LLMs, in models ranging from 70 million to 2.8 billion parameters. We find that task abilities and the functional components that support them emerge consistently at similar token counts across scale. Moreover, although such components may be implemented by different attention heads over time, the overarching algorithm that they implement remains. Surprisingly, both these algorithms and the types of components involved therein can replicate across model scale. These results suggest that circuit analyses conducted on small models at the end of pre-training can provide insights that still apply after additional pre-training and over model scale.

papers.title: Towards Vision-Language Mechanistic Interpretability: A Causal Tracing Tool for BLIP
papers.research_question: How can causal mediation analysis be adapted to vision-language models to study neural mechanisms in BLIP for visual question answering?
papers.core_contribution: Adapts causal tracing to vision-language models, specifically BLIP, for studying neural mechanisms in visual question answering, and releases an open-source tool.
papers.conclusion: Introduces the first causal tracing tool for vision-language models, demonstrating its application on BLIP for VQA, and opens up future research in vision-language mechanistic interpretability.
papers.key_findings:
Final layers in the question encoder and answer decoder are most causally relevant for correct answers in VQA.
The noise factor ν affects probability recovery, with a decaying curve as ν increases.
BLIP may process vision and language independently in intermediate layers, or final layers override preceding layers.
papers.limitation: The role of the noise factor ν is unclear, and performance is not monotonically reduced by increasing ν.
future_direction: Study why different components have different sensitivities to noise.
Investigate cross-module coordination by restoring multiple points.
Identify larger mechanisms in vision-language models for tasks like compositional understanding.
papers.abstract: Mechanistic interpretability seeks to understand the neural mechanisms that enable specific behaviors in Large Language Models (LLMs) by leveraging causality-based methods. While these approaches have identified neural circuits that copy spans of text, capture factual knowledge, and more, they remain unusable for multimodal models since adapting these tools to the vision-language domain requires considerable architectural changes. In this work, we adapt a unimodal causal tracing tool to BLIP to enable the study of the neural mechanisms underlying image-conditioned text generation. We demonstrate our approach on a visual question answering dataset, highlighting the causal relevance of later layer representations for all tokens. Furthermore, we release our BLIP causal tracing tool as open source to enable further experimentation in vision-language mechanistic interpretability by the community. Our code is available at https://github.com/vedantpalit/Towards-Vision-Language-Mechanistic-Interpretability.

papers.title: Extending Token Computation for LLM Reasoning
papers.research_question: What is the effect of increased computed tokens on LLM performance? Can extending the Chain-of-Thought chain within the same prompt improve reasoning outcomes?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces a novel algorithm that extends computed tokens in the Chain-of-Thought process by optimizing attention mechanisms, which improves reasoning capabilities, especially in non-STEM domains.
papers.conclusion: The study introduces an attention optimization method that enhances LLM reasoning, particularly in non-STEM domains, and sets the groundwork for more transparent and adaptable models for real-world applications.
papers.key_findings:
Increasing the number of computed tokens enhances LLM reasoning performance.
Attention patterns in middle layers are skewed by non-semantic tokens with high attention scores, which hinders reasoning.
The proposed algorithm re-balances attention distributions by emulating early layer attention patterns, leading to more extended and logical reasoning steps.
The method improves reasoning in non-STEM domains but may reduce accuracy in memory-dependent questions due to error propagation.
Larger models (e.g., 13B) show greater improvement with the method compared to smaller models (e.g., 7B).
papers.limitation:
The method reduces accuracy by 3 percentage points in memory-dependent questions from the MMLU dataset.
Extended reasoning may amplify error propagation in STEM categories where the model's reasoning capabilities are not robust.
Scarcity of logical process examples for STEM questions in training data may hinder performance.
future_direction: Integrate a training phase to enhance memory recall for early-answering questions.
Reduce memory and computational demands using techniques like ghost attention mechanisms.
Enhance interpretability of attention patterns across layers.
papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) are pivotal in advancing natural language processing but often struggle with complex reasoning tasks due to inefficient attention distributions. In this paper, we explore the effect of increased computed tokens on LLM performance and introduce a novel method for extending computed tokens in the Chain-of-Thought (CoT) process, utilizing attention mechanism optimization. By fine-tuning an LLM on a domain-specific, highly structured dataset, we analyze attention patterns across layers, identifying inefficiencies caused by non-semantic tokens with outlier high attention scores. To address this, we propose an algorithm that emulates early layer attention patterns across downstream layers to re-balance skewed attention distributions and enhance knowledge abstraction. Our findings demonstrate that our approach not only facilitates a deeper understanding of the internal dynamics of LLMs but also significantly improves their reasoning capabilities, particularly in non-STEM domains. Our study lays the groundwork for further innovations in LLM design, aiming to create more powerful, versatile, and responsible models capable of tackling a broad range of real-world applications.

papers.title: Inducing Systematicity in Transformers by Attending to Structurally Quantized Embeddings
papers.research_question: How to induce systematicity in Transformers with low-complexity training data to improve compositional generalization?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes SQ-Transformer, which uses Structure-oriented Vector Quantization (SoVQ) and systematic attention layers (SAL/SRL) to induce systematicity and improve compositional generalization in Transformers.
papers.conclusion: SQ-Transformer effectively induces systematicity in Transformers and improves compositional generalization, providing insights into the inner mechanisms of Transformers and laying groundwork for future architecture design.
papers.key_findings:
SQ-Transformer achieves stronger compositional generalization than vanilla Transformer on multiple low-complexity semantic parsing and machine translation datasets.
SoVQ learns a syntactically clustered embedding space.
SAL/SRL induce generalizable attention patterns that lead to improved systematicity.
SQ-Transformer with SAL works well on small synthetic datasets, while SRL is better for larger natural datasets.
The method is effective even without data augmentation or large pretraining.
papers.limitation: SQ-Transformer does not explicitly encourage phrasal constituents with the same syntactic role to be close in representation space, limiting performance on deeper recursion and novel combinations of grammatical structures and phrasal constituents.
future_direction: Handling phrasal constituents and deeper recursion in compositional generalization.
papers.abstract: Transformers generalize to novel compositions of structures and entities after being trained on a complex dataset, but easily overfit on datasets of insufficient complexity. We observe that when the training set is sufficiently complex, the model encodes sentences that have a common syntactic structure using a systematic attention pattern. Inspired by this observation, we propose SQ-Transformer (Structurally Quantized) that explicitly encourages systematicity in the embeddings and attention layers, even with a training set of low complexity. At the embedding level, we introduce Structure-oriented Vector Quantization (SoVQ) to cluster word embeddings into several classes of structurally equivalent entities. At the attention level, we devise the Systematic Attention Layer (SAL) and an alternative, Systematically Regularized Layer (SRL) that operate on the quantized word embeddings so that sentences of the same structure are encoded with invariant or similar attention patterns. Empirically, we show that SQ-Transformer achieves stronger compositional generalization than the vanilla Transformer on multiple low-complexity semantic parsing and machine translation datasets. In our analysis, we show that SoVQ indeed learns a syntactically clustered embedding space and SAL/SRL induces generalizable attention patterns, which lead to improved systematicity.

papers.title: Uncovering Emergent Physics Representations Learned In-Context by Large Language Models
papers.research_question: Do large language models implicitly learn physics during in-context learning, and do recognizable physical quantities emerge as distinct features in their internal representations?
papers.core_contribution: This paper shows that large language models can learn to forecast physical dynamics via in-context learning, and that energy-related features emerge in their residual stream activations, which are causally important for accurate predictions.
papers.conclusion: The results demonstrate that LLMs can internalize physical concepts like energy during in-context learning, suggesting transformer architectures can internalize abstract reasoning priors similar to human abstraction.
papers.key_findings:
Prediction accuracy for physical dynamics forecasting improves with longer context length.
Sparse activations from sparse autoencoders (SAEs) applied to residual streams correlate with energy quantities (total, kinetic, potential).
The correlation between sparse activations and energy is context-dependent and increases with longer contexts, especially for chaotic systems.
Intervention experiments ablating energy-correlated sparse activations degrade prediction accuracy, indicating their functional role.
Energy-related features are most prominently captured in the middle layers of the transformer.
papers.limitation: The study uses raw trajectory values as the sole input modality without external instructions or prompting strategies, leaving open whether chain-of-thought or structured prompts would strengthen correlations.
future_direction: Explore physics concepts beyond classical mechanics.
Investigate more human-aligned tasks such as answering conceptual questions from physics exams.
Leverage physics-informed tasks to understand internal mechanisms of large-scale models and advance LLM-based agents for physically realistic environments.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) exhibit impressive in-context learning (ICL) abilities, enabling them to solve wide range of tasks via textual prompts alone. As these capabilities advance, the range of applicable domains continues to expand significantly. However, identifying the precise mechanisms or internal structures within LLMs that allow successful ICL across diverse, distinct classes of tasks remains elusive. Physics-based tasks offer a promising testbed for probing this challenge. Unlike synthetic sequences such as basic arithmetic or symbolic equations, physical systems provide experimentally controllable, real-world data based on structured dynamics grounded in fundamental principles. This makes them particularly suitable for studying the emergent reasoning behaviors of LLMs in a realistic yet tractable setting. Here, we mechanistically investigate the ICL ability of LLMs, especially focusing on their ability to reason about physics. Using a dynamics forecasting task in physical systems as a proxy, we evaluate whether LLMs can learn physics in context. We first show that the performance of dynamics forecasting in context improves with longer input contexts. To uncover how such capability emerges in LLMs, we analyze the model's residual stream activations using sparse autoencoders (SAEs). Our experiments reveal that the features captured by SAEs correlate with key physical variables, such as energy. These findings demonstrate that meaningful physical concepts are encoded within LLMs during in-context learning. In sum, our work provides a novel case study that broadens our understanding of how LLMs learn in context.

papers.title: Efficiently Democratizing Medical LLMs for 50 Languages via a Mixture of Language Family Experts
papers.research_question: How to efficiently adapt medical Large Language Models to many languages, especially low-resource ones, by analyzing internal information flow and using language family experts?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes an efficient method to scale medical LLMs to 50 languages via language family experts and a Post-MoE architecture, based on the discovery of the 'Spread Out in the End' information flow mechanism.
papers.conclusion: The proposed Apollo-MoE method efficiently democratizes medical LLMs to 50 languages, demonstrating strong generalization and scalability.
papers.key_findings:
Discovered the 'Spread Out in the End' mechanism in multilingual MoE models: early layers concentrate cross-lingual information flow, later layers exhibit language-specific divergence.
Proposed Post-MoE architecture (MoE only in later layers) improves generalization to low-resource languages.
Introduced language family experts, enabling scaling to many languages without adding parameters.
Hybrid-k routing (language-specific experts with cross-lingual routing) outperforms Top-k and Language-Specific routing.
papers.abstract: Adapting medical Large Language Models to local languages can reduce barriers to accessing healthcare services, but data scarcity remains a significant challenge, particularly for low-resource languages. To address this, we first construct a high-quality medical dataset and conduct analysis to ensure its quality. In order to leverage the generalization capability of multilingual LLMs to efficiently scale to more resource-constrained languages, we explore the internal information flow of LLMs from a multilingual perspective using Mixture of Experts (MoE) modularity. Technically, we propose a novel MoE routing method that employs language-specific experts and cross-lingual routing. Inspired by circuit theory, our routing analysis revealed a Spread Out in the End information flow mechanism: while earlier layers concentrate cross-lingual information flow, the later layers exhibit language-specific divergence. This insight directly led to the development of the Post-MoE architecture, which applies sparse routing only in the later layers while maintaining dense others. Experimental results demonstrate that this approach enhances the generalization of multilingual models to other languages while preserving interpretability. Finally, to efficiently scale the model to 50 languages, we introduce the concept of language family experts, drawing on linguistic priors, which enables scaling the number of languages without adding additional parameters.

papers.title: Interpreting vision transformers via residual replacement model
papers.research_question: How do vision transformers (ViTs) represent and process the world?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces the residual replacement model, which replaces ViT computations with interpretable SAE features in the residual stream, enabling scalable circuit discovery and application to debiasing spurious correlations.
papers.conclusion: The residual replacement model provides a faithful and interpretable framework for understanding ViT mechanisms, with practical utility in tasks like debiasing.
papers.key_findings:
SAE features in ViTs are interpretable across all layers, evolving from low-level attributes to high-level semantic concepts.
ViTs encode specialized features such as curve detectors and position detectors, analogous to those in CNNs and LMs.
The residual replacement model produces parsimonious circuits that faithfully explain ViT mechanisms, with improvements from edge-based discovery and gradient correction.
The framework enables quantitative analysis of feature similarity across layers, showing convergence for intra-class images.
The model can be applied to debias spurious correlations in ImageNet classifiers through feature ablation.
future_direction: Incorporating higher-order interactions between intermediate features in the gradient-based decomposition.
papers.abstract: How do vision transformers (ViTs) represent and process the world? This paper addresses this long-standing question through the first systematic analysis of 6.6K features across all layers, extracted via sparse autoencoders, and by introducing the residual replacement model, which replaces ViT computations with interpretable features in the residual stream. Our analysis reveals not only a feature evolution from low-level patterns to high-level semantics, but also how ViTs encode curves and spatial positions through specialized feature types. The residual replacement model scalably produces a faithful yet parsimonious circuit for human-scale interpretability by significantly simplifying the original computations. As a result, this framework enables intuitive understanding of ViT mechanisms. Finally, we demonstrate the utility of our framework in debiasing spurious correlations.

papers.title: Transformer visualization via dictionary learning: contextualized embedding as a linear superposition of transformer factors
papers.research_question: How can dictionary learning be used to visualize and interpret the hierarchical semantic structures captured in transformer networks?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes using dictionary learning to factorize contextualized word embeddings from transformer layers into sparse linear combinations of 'transformer factors', which reveal hierarchical semantic structures like word-level disambiguation, sentence-level patterns, and long-range dependencies.
papers.conclusion: Dictionary learning provides a powerful visualization tool for transformer networks, revealing hierarchical semantic and syntactic representations learned at different layers and offering new insights into model behavior.
papers.key_findings:
Transformer factors capture word-level polysemy disambiguation, with disambiguation developing progressively across layers.
Mid-level transformer factors capture sentence-level patterns such as consecutive adjectives and unit exchange.
High-level transformer factors capture long-range dependencies like repetitive patterns and the structure of biography beginnings.
Importance score curves show that features learned in early layers persist with decay in later layers, and abstract features develop gradually.
Dictionary learning can reveal linguistic patterns beyond prior knowledge, complementing probing tasks.
future_direction: Apply dictionary learning to other neural network architectures with skip connections, such as ResNet and Vision Transformers (ViT).
Adapt transformer-specific interpretation tools (e.g., from Chefer et al.) for better visualization of token contributions.
papers.abstract: Transformer networks have revolutionized NLP representation learning since they were introduced. Though a great effort has been made to explain the representation in transformers, it is widely recognized that our understanding is not sufficient. One important reason is that there lack enough visualization tools for detailed analysis. In this paper, we propose to use dictionary learning to open up these 'black boxes' as linear superpositions of transformer factors. Through visualization, we demonstrate the hierarchical semantic structures captured by the transformer factors, e.g., word-level polysemy disambiguation, sentence-level pattern formation, and long-range dependency. While some of these patterns confirm the conventional prior linguistic knowledge, the rest are relatively unexpected, which may provide new insights. We hope this visualization tool can bring further knowledge and a better understanding of how transformer networks work.

papers.title: Same Task, Different Circuits: Disentangling Modality-Specific Mechanisms in VLMs
papers.research_question: Why do Vision-Language models (VLMs) perform worse on visual tasks compared to analogous textual tasks?
papers.core_contribution: VLMs use largely disjoint circuits for visual and textual tasks, but the functional difference lies in data processing; patching visual token embeddings from later layers to earlier layers (back-patching) reduces the performance gap without training.
papers.conclusion: The performance gap in VLMs arises from disjoint circuits for different modalities, and back-patching provides a training-free method to reduce it by aligning visual representations earlier.
papers.key_findings:
Vision and language circuits are structurally disjoint but implement similar functionalities for query and generation.
The performance gap stems from differences in processing modality-specific data tokens.
Visual token representations become aligned with textual counterparts only in later layers.
Back-patching visual token embeddings from later to earlier layers improves visual task accuracy, closing about a third of the performance gap on average.
The intervention is effective across multiple models and tasks.
papers.limitation:
Focused on single-image question-answering tasks with single-token completions.
Current open models struggle with complex visual reasoning, limiting analysis.
Circuit analysis methods are limited to single-token completions.
Back-patching closes only 32% of the performance gap; causes for the remaining gap are unclear.
Analysis is limited to adapter-based VLMs; may not apply to other fusion approaches.
future_direction: Explore multi-image scenarios, different prompt orders, and more complex visual reasoning tasks.
Investigate varied computational resources per token, especially for visual inputs.
Extend analysis to VLMs with different fusion approaches.
papers.abstract: Vision-Language models (VLMs) show impressive abilities to answer questions on visual inputs (e.g., counting objects in an image), yet demonstrate higher accuracies when performing an analogous task on text (e.g., counting words in a text). We investigate this accuracy gap by identifying and comparing the \textit{circuits} - the task-specific computational sub-graphs - in different modalities. We show that while circuits are largely disjoint between modalities, they implement relatively similar functionalities: the differences lie primarily in processing modality-specific data positions (an image or a text sequence). Zooming in on the image data representations, we observe they become aligned with the higher-performing analogous textual representations only towards later layers, too late in processing to effectively influence subsequent positions. To overcome this, we patch the representations of visual data tokens from later layers back into earlier layers. In experiments with multiple tasks and models, this simple intervention closes a third of the performance gap between the modalities, on average. Our analysis sheds light on the multi-modal performance gap in VLMs and suggests a training-free approach for reducing it.

papers.title: Why Linear Interpretability Works: Invariant Subspaces as a Result of Architectural Constraints
papers.research_question: Why do linear interpretability methods like linear probes and sparse autoencoders succeed in deep nonlinear transformer models?
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that linear interpretability methods succeed because transformer architectures have linear communication interfaces (attention OV circuits and unembedding matrices), which force semantic features to occupy context-invariant linear subspaces. It introduces the Self-Reference Property, where tokens provide the geometric directions for their associated features, enabling zero-shot semantic classification.
papers.conclusion: Linear interpretability in transformers is a structural consequence of architectural constraints, not merely an empirical regularity. The Self-Reference Property enables zero-shot semantic classification without labeled data.
papers.key_findings:
The Invariant Subspace Necessity theorem establishes that any semantic feature decoded through a linear interface must lie in a context-invariant subspace.
The Self-Reference Property shows that tokens directly provide the invariant geometric directions for their associated features.
Empirical validation across eight classification tasks and four model families confirms that class tokens align with instance directions, supporting directional invariance.
Zero-shot, unsupervised, and sparse autoencoder-based probes all recover the same directional structure, providing converging evidence.
Polysemy (one token with multiple directions) and partial synonymy (multiple tokens sharing a direction) are two sides of the same coin in the geometric representation.
papers.limitation:
The framework focuses on features communicated through linear interfaces; features operating through nonlinear gating (e.g., QK routing) may not exhibit the same invariance.
The work does not characterize when invariant subspaces collapse to single directions versus higher-dimensional structures.
future_direction: The Self-Reference Property suggests paths toward scalable, unsupervised circuit discovery.
The connection between sparse autoencoder features and token directions offers new evaluation criteria for dictionary learning.
papers.abstract: Linear probes and sparse autoencoders consistently recover meaningful structure from transformer representations -- yet why should such simple methods succeed in deep, nonlinear systems? We show this is not merely an empirical regularity but a consequence of architectural necessity: transformers communicate information through linear interfaces (attention OV circuits, unembedding matrices), and any semantic feature decoded through such an interface must occupy a context-invariant linear subspace. We formalize this as the \emph{Invariant Subspace Necessity} theorem and derive the \emph{Self-Reference Property}: tokens directly provide the geometric direction for their associated features, enabling zero-shot identification of semantic structure without labeled data or learned probes. Empirical validation in eight classification tasks and four model families confirms the alignment between class tokens and semantically related instances. Our framework provides \textbf{a principled architectural explanation} for why linear interpretability methods work, unifying linear probes and sparse autoencoders.

papers.title: Calibrating LLM Confidence by Probing Perturbed Representation Stability
papers.research_question: How can we improve LLM confidence estimation by analyzing the stability of internal representations under targeted adversarial perturbations?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces CCPS, a method that estimates LLM confidence by analyzing the stability of internal representations under adversarial perturbations, achieving significant improvements in calibration and discrimination metrics across diverse models and benchmarks.
papers.conclusion: CCPS provides an efficient, accurate, and generalizable method for LLM confidence estimation, enhancing the trustworthiness of LLMs in critical domains.
papers.key_findings:
CCPS reduces average Expected Calibration Error by approximately 55% (up to 88%) and Brier score by 21% (up to 45%) compared to the best baseline.
CCPS increases average Accuracy by 5 percentage points, AUCPR by 4 percentage points, and AUROC by 6 percentage points.
CCPS generalizes across diverse LLM architectures (Llama, Qwen, Mistral) and model scales (8B to 32B parameters).
CCPS performs well on both multiple-choice and open-ended question answering formats.
CCPS is parameter-efficient, adding only around 9.5k trainable parameters, compared to baselines that may add millions.
papers.abstract: Reza Khanmohammadi, Erfan Miahi, Mehrsa Mardikoraem, Simerjot Kaur, Ivan Brugere, Charese Smiley, Kundan S Thind, Mohammad M. Ghassemi. Proceedings of the 2025 Conference on Empirical Methods in Natural Language Processing. 2025.

papers.title: Studying Cross-cluster Modularity in Neural Networks
papers.research_question: What are the effects of training neural networks to be modular using a clusterability loss on interpretability, such as task specialization and circuit size?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces a clusterability measure and loss function to train neural networks to be modular. Shows that modular models do not exhibit more task specialization but have smaller circuits, aiding interpretability.
papers.conclusion: A simple regularizer can split neural network layers into non-interacting modules, but these modules do not yield expected interpretability benefits like task specialization. However, modularity improves circuit size and search space without performance loss.
papers.key_findings:
Pre-trained models are not modular; clusters are highly enmeshed.
Training with clusterability loss effectively increases modularity in models.
Modular models do not show increased task specialization compared to non-modular models.
Modular models have smaller effective circuits, reducing circuit size.
Theoretical analysis indicates modularity simplifies function spaces and reduces the number of features.
papers.limitation: The modularity metric does not lead to clear interpretability benefits such as task specialization.
future_direction: Investigate alternative regularizers for interpretability benefits.
Build an automated subtask detection mechanism.
papers.abstract: An approach to improve neural network interpretability is via clusterability, i.e., splitting a model into disjoint clusters that can be studied independently. We define a measure for clusterability and show that pre-trained models form highly enmeshed clusters via spectral graph clustering. We thus train models to be more modular using a "clusterability loss" function that encourages the formation of non-interacting clusters. We then investigate the emerging properties of these highly clustered models. We find our trained clustered models do not exhibit more task specialization, but do form smaller circuits. We investigate CNNs trained on MNIST and CIFAR, small transformers trained on modular addition, and GPT-2 and Pythia on the Wiki dataset, and Gemma on a Chemistry dataset. This investigation shows what to expect from clustered models.

papers.title: Transformers as Multi-task Learners: Decoupling Features in Hidden Markov Models
papers.research_question: How do Transformers achieve multi-task generalization? Specifically, what are the layerwise mechanisms by which they represent and process sequential information?
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that Transformers learn local features in lower layers and decoupled, temporally disentangled features in upper layers when modeling Hidden Markov Models, and provides theoretical constructions that align with these observations.
papers.conclusion: This work advances theoretical and empirical understanding of how Transformers achieve strong generalization across sequence learning tasks, showing they transition from local feature learning in lower layers to decoupled representations in upper layers, providing a principled explanation for their expressiveness and efficiency in multi-task and in-context learning.
papers.key_findings:
Well-trained Transformers achieve high accuracy under in-context learning on HMMs, with performance improving as more input-output examples are provided or as sequence length increases.
Lower layers of Transformers focus on learning local representations, primarily influenced by neighboring tokens.
Upper layers develop decoupled, temporally disentangled representations that are less tied to specific input positions and encode higher-level abstractions.
Transformers gradually recognize task identity across layers, with hidden state identification occurring earlier than task identification, indicating a layerwise processing hierarchy.
The theoretical construction demonstrates that Transformers can approximate low-rank HMMs using a fixed-length memory structure, enabling effective in-context learning.
papers.limitation: Analysis is limited to Hidden Markov Models and may not generalize to more complex settings.
future_direction: Extend analysis to more general assumptions and more complex model settings.
papers.abstract: Transformer based models have shown remarkable capabilities in sequence learning across a wide range of tasks, often performing well on specific task by leveraging input-output examples. Despite their empirical success, a comprehensive theoretical understanding of this phenomenon remains limited. In this work, we investigate the layerwise behavior of Transformers to uncover the mechanisms underlying their multi-task generalization ability. Taking explorations on a typical sequence model, i.e, Hidden Markov Models, which are fundamental to many language tasks, we observe that: first, lower layers of Transformers focus on extracting feature representations, primarily influenced by neighboring tokens; second, on the upper layers, features become decoupled, exhibiting a high degree of time disentanglement. Building on these empirical insights, we provide theoretical analysis for the expressiveness power of Transformers. Our explicit constructions align closely with empirical observations, providing theoretical support for the Transformer's effectiveness and efficiency on sequence learning across diverse tasks.

papers.title: Can abstract concepts from LLM improve SLM performance?
papers.research_question: Can the sophisticated concepts learned by large, powerful models be extracted and used to enhance smaller language models?
papers.core_contribution: The paper proposes a cross-architecture framework to transfer conceptual knowledge (steering vectors) from a large source model to a smaller target model during inference, and introduces inference-time scaling to dynamically adjust steering intensity, leading to performance improvements without fine-tuning.
papers.conclusion: The proposed cross-architecture framework effectively transfers conceptual knowledge via steering vectors, acting as a 'conceptual booster' to enhance smaller, more efficient models without costly fine-tuning.
papers.key_findings:
Steering vectors extracted from a large source model can be transferred to smaller target models from different architectural families, leading to consistent performance improvements across diverse reasoning tasks.
The performance gains are architecture-agnostic, observed across various model families (Llama, Gemma, Qwen) and datasets (GSM8K, MATH, ARC-C).
Inference-time scaling (running the model across a range of steering coefficients and taking the mode) provides an additional performance uplift, with gains of 7-15% for the smallest model (Qwen3-0.6B).
The steering vectors are architecture-specific, with negligible correlation between the primary directions of variance extracted from different parent models.
Performance is robust at lower steering intensities (λ <= 0.3) but degrades at higher values, and the robustness varies with child model architecture (e.g., Gemma models are more resilient than Llama models).
papers.limitation:
The framework uses a greedy n->n layer mapping between source and target models, which is sub-optimal. The optimal alignment of concepts across different network depths remains an open question.
Using a single λ value for the entire model is greedy and depends on the validation dataset; in reality, λ should be a function of model depth and layer index.
future_direction: Exploring a more sophisticated, cross-architecture layer-mapping strategy.
Dynamically figuring out λ per layer instead of using a single value for the entire model.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) excel at diverse tasks, but their deployment on resource-constrained devices remains challenging. Existing methods like quantization, pruning, and distillation can reduce memory footprint but often demand extensive experimentation and careful infrastructure design. Leveraging existing techniques for extracting high-level concepts (represented as steering vectors) from larger models, we investigate their transferability to smaller language models (SLM) during inference. We demonstrate through extensive experimentation that these concepts can be effectively transferred to smaller models, irrespective of their family (e.g., Phi, Llama, Qwen), leading to performance improvements across a wide range of tasks. Furthermore, we introduce inference-time scaling to enhance performance by dynamically adjusting the steering intensity which has resulted in a 7-15\% of accuracy improvement for Qwen3-0.6B.

papers.title: DePass: Unified Feature Attributing by Simple Decomposed Forward Pass
papers.research_question: How can we attribute the behavior of Transformer models to internal computations in a faithful, fine-grained, and unified way without requiring auxiliary training?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces DePass, a unified framework for feature attribution in Transformers based on a single decomposed forward pass that freezes attention scores and MLP activations, enabling lossless, additive decomposition and faithful attribution without auxiliary training.
papers.conclusion: DePass is a simple and efficient framework for interpreting Transformer models via a decomposed forward pass, achieving faithful attribution across token-level, component-level, and subspace-level granularities and serving as a general-purpose tool for mechanistic interpretability.
papers.key_findings:
DePass enables lossless additive decomposition of hidden states throughout the forward pass of Transformer models.
DePass provides more faithful token-level attribution compared to gradient-based and attention-based baseline methods.
DePass can attribute model behavior to specific architectural components (attention heads, MLP neurons) and to arbitrary linear subspaces.
DePass can be combined with Sparse Autoencoders (SAE) for token-level attribution of interpretable features.
DePass is computationally efficient, requiring only a single forward pass and significantly faster than exhaustive ablation methods.
papers.limitation:
DePass only captures information flow through the output-value (OV) circuit and does not explain query-key (QK) circuit interactions.
Decomposing the QK circuit would involve quadratic complexity and remains a challenging open problem.
Practical memory constraints require grouping components for fine-grained analysis, which can increase time costs.
future_direction: Unwrapping the QK circuit to understand its interactions is a key direction for future work.
Releasing a general-purpose toolkit supporting a broad range of Transformer models.
Optimizing computational efficiency and improving hardware deployment strategies to support higher-resolution attribution.
papers.abstract: Attributing the behavior of Transformer models to internal computations is a central challenge in mechanistic interpretability. We introduce DePass, a unified framework for feature attribution based on a single decomposed forward pass. DePass decomposes hidden states into customized additive components, then propagates them with attention scores and MLP's activations fixed. It achieves faithful, fine-grained attribution without requiring auxiliary training. We validate DePass across token-level, model component-level, and subspace-level attribution tasks, demonstrating its effectiveness and fidelity. Our experiments highlight its potential to attribute information flow between arbitrary components of a Transformer model. We hope DePass serves as a foundational tool for broader applications in interpretability.

papers.title: Inverting Supervised Representations with Autoregressive Neural Density Models
papers.research_question: How can we invert supervised representations to gain insights into the invariances learned by models and to estimate the mutual information between inputs and intermediate representations?
papers.core_contribution: Presents a method for inverting supervised representations using autoregressive neural density models, enabling visualization of model invariances and estimation of mutual information between inputs and intermediate representations.
papers.conclusion: The method facilitates visualization of model invariances and provides a scalable quantitative estimate of the amount of information preserved by a network.
papers.key_findings:
Mutual information between inputs and network layers decreases through successive layers, with the biggest reduction between CONV1 and CONV2.
Global pooling induces translation invariance in convolutional networks, while preserving style and rotation information.
Mutual information initially increases and then decreases over the course of training, supporting the information bottleneck theory.
Inversion models provide better calibration of variability compared to SGAN and nearest neighbor methods.
The method allows analysis of architectural choices by revealing invariances learned by different network architectures.
papers.limitation: Density estimation is challenging in higher dimensions, and it is not known how well a given model represents the true density.
future_direction: Improving the method as neural density models improve to achieve tighter mutual information bounds and more representative samples.
papers.abstract: We present a method for feature interpretation that makes use of recent advances in autoregressive density estimation models to invert model representations. We train generative inversion models to express a distribution over input features conditioned on intermediate model representations. Insights into the invariances learned by supervised models can be gained by viewing samples from these inversion models. In addition, we can use these inversion models to estimate the mutual information between a model’s inputs and its intermediate representations, thus quantifying the amount of information preserved by the network at different stages. Using this method we examine the types of information preserved at different layers of convolutional neural networks, and explore the invariances induced by different architectural choices. Finally we show that the mutual information between inputs and network layers initially increases and then decreases over the course of training, supporting recent work by Shwartz-Ziv and Tishby (2017) on the information bottleneck theory of deep learning.

papers.title: A Mechanistic Interpretation of Arithmetic Reasoning in Language Models using Causal Mediation Analysis
papers.research_question: How do language models process and store information related to arithmetic tasks? What model components are responsible for arithmetic reasoning?
papers.core_contribution: Language models process arithmetic queries by transferring operand and operator information from early layers to the last token via attention, and then late MLP modules generate result-related information and incorporate it into the residual stream.
papers.conclusion: Causal mediation analysis reveals the mechanistic process of arithmetic reasoning in LMs, suggesting avenues for model pruning and targeted training.
papers.key_findings:
The model conveys operand and operator information from early layers to the last token using attention mechanisms.
Late MLP modules at the last token incorporate result-related information into the residual stream.
The activation patterns are specific to arithmetic queries compared to number retrieval and factual knowledge tasks.
The relative importance of late MLPs is high for arithmetic but low for other tasks.
Neuron-level interventions show that the top neurons for arithmetic overlap partially with number retrieval and not more than random with factual knowledge.
papers.limitation:
The study is limited to the four fundamental arithmetic operators.
The queries are synthetically generated and not from real-life math word problems.
The analysis does not break down attention into individual heads.
future_direction: Study a broader set of mathematical operators.
Expand analysis to real-life math word problems.
Identify specific attention heads responsible for forwarding information.
papers.abstract: Mathematical reasoning in large language models (LMs) has garnered significant attention in recent work, but there is a limited understanding of how these models process and store information related to arithmetic tasks within their architecture. In order to improve our understanding of this aspect of language models, we present a mechanistic interpretation of Transformer-based LMs on arithmetic questions using a causal mediation analysis framework. By intervening on the activations of specific model components and measuring the resulting changes in predicted probabilities, we identify the subset of parameters responsible for specific predictions. This provides insights into how information related to arithmetic is processed by LMs. Our experimental results indicate that LMs process the input by transmitting the information relevant to the query from mid-sequence early layers to the final token using the attention mechanism. Then, this information is processed by a set of MLP modules, which generate result-related information that is incorporated into the residual stream. To assess the specificity of the observed activation dynamics, we compare the effects of different model components on arithmetic queries with other tasks, including number retrieval from prompts and factual knowledge questions.

papers.title: XAI for Transformers: Better Explanations through Conservative Propagation
papers.research_question: How to bring Explainable AI to Transformers in a theoretically sound manner, focusing on the axiom of conservation to reliably identify the contribution of input features to the prediction.
papers.core_contribution: Proposes a theoretically grounded extension of Layer-wise Relevance Propagation (LRP) to Transformers by addressing conservation issues in attention heads and LayerNorm, leading to state-of-the-art explanation performance.
papers.conclusion: The proposed LRP-based explanation method for Transformers addresses conservation issues and achieves state-of-the-art performance, contributing to safer and more transparent use of Transformers.
papers.key_findings:
Gradient×Input fails to conserve relevance in Transformers due to attention heads and LayerNorm.
The proposed LRP rules (detaching gating and rescaling terms) restore conservation.
The proposed method outperforms existing explanation methods on a variety of Transformer models and datasets.
The method can be used to analyze bias in models without generating counterfactual examples.
papers.abstract: Transformers have become an important workhorse of machine learning, with numerous applications. This necessitates the development of reliable methods for increasing their transparency. Multiple interpretability methods, often based on gradient information, have been proposed. We show that the gradient in a Transformer reflects the function only locally, and thus fails to reliably identify the contribution of input features to the prediction. We identify Attention Heads and LayerNorm as main reasons for such unreliable explanations and propose a more stable way for propagation through these layers. Our proposal, which can be seen as a proper extension of the well-established LRP method to Transformers, is shown both theoretically and empirically to overcome the deficiency of a simple gradient-based approach, and achieves state-of-the-art explanation performance on a broad range of Transformer models and datasets.

papers.title: Towards Principled Evaluations of Sparse Autoencoders for Interpretability and Control
papers.research_question: How to evaluate sparse autoencoders for interpretability and control in the context of specific tasks, by comparing them against supervised feature dictionaries.
papers.core_contribution: Proposes a framework for evaluating sparse autoencoders using supervised feature dictionaries as a benchmark, applied to the IOI task.
papers.conclusion: The framework provides a step towards more objective evaluations of sparse dictionary learning methods.
papers.key_findings:
SAEs capture interpretable features for the IOI task but are less successful than supervised features in controlling the model.
Feature occlusion and feature over-splitting phenomena are observed in SAE training.
papers.limitation: The F1 score does not take into account the magnitude of feature activations and is a conservative metric.
future_direction: Address limitations of the F1 score in interpretability evaluations
papers.abstract: Disentangling model activations into meaningful features is a central problem in interpretability. However, the absence of ground-truth for these features in realistic scenarios makes validating recent approaches, such as sparse dictionary learning, elusive. To address this challenge, we propose a framework for evaluating feature dictionaries in the context of specific tasks, by comparing them against \emph{supervised} feature dictionaries. First, we demonstrate that supervised dictionaries achieve excellent approximation, control, and interpretability of model computations on the task. Second, we use the supervised dictionaries to develop and contextualize evaluations of unsupervised dictionaries along the same three axes. We apply this framework to the indirect object identification (IOI) task using GPT-2 Small, with sparse autoencoders (SAEs) trained on either the IOI or OpenWebText datasets. We find that these SAEs capture interpretable features for the IOI task, but they are less successful than supervised features in controlling the model. Finally, we observe two qualitative phenomena in SAE training: feature occlusion (where a causally relevant concept is robustly overshadowed by even slightly higher-magnitude ones in the learned features), and feature over-splitting (where binary features split into many smaller, less interpretable features). We hope that our framework will provide a useful step towards more objective and grounded evaluations of sparse dictionary learning methods.

papers.title: LinEAS: End-to-end Learning of Activation Steering with a Distributional Loss
papers.research_question: How can we efficiently control generative models by steering activations with a global distributional loss that requires low data and is modality-agnostic?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces LinEAS, a method for activation steering that uses a global distributional loss to jointly learn affine transformations across layers, enabling effective control with low data and automatic neuron selection via sparsity regularization.
papers.conclusion: LinEAS is an effective method for activation steering, offering improved controllability and robustness by learning lightweight interventions with a global distributional loss.
papers.key_findings:
LinEAS outperforms existing activation steering methods on toxicity mitigation in LLMs and style control in text-to-image models.
LinEAS requires only a handful of unpaired samples (e.g., 32) to be effective.
The global loss and joint optimization across layers lead to more robust interventions and better preservation of model utility.
Sparsity regularization allows automatic selection of neurons and layers, reducing the intervention support by 100x.
LinEAS provides a continuous intervention strength parameter, allowing fine-grained control.
papers.limitation: The method requires access to intermediate activations, which may not be available in all settings.
future_direction: Extending LinEAS to other modalities and tasks.
Investigating the theoretical properties of the distributional loss.
papers.abstract: The growing use of generative models in daily life calls for efficient mechanisms to control their generation, to e.g., produce safe content or provide users with tools to explore style changes. Ideally, such mechanisms should require low volume of unpaired data (i.e., without explicit preference), and should be cheap, both at train and inference time, while preserving output quality. Recent research has shown that such mechanisms can be obtained by intervening exclusively on model activations, with the goal of correcting distributional differences between activations seen when using prompts from a source vs. a target set (e.g., toxic and non-toxic sentences). While cheap, these fast methods are inherently crude: their maps are tuned locally, not accounting for their impact on downstream layers, resulting in interventions that cause unintended shifts when used out-of-sample. We propose in this work linear end-to-end activation steering (LinEAS), an approach trained with a global loss that accounts simultaneously for all layer-wise distributional shifts. In addition to being more robust, the loss used to train LinEAS can be regularized with sparsifying norms, which can automatically carry out neuron selection. LinEAS only requires a handful of unpaired samples to be effective, and beats similar baselines on toxicity mitigation in language models, becoming competitive with oracle-dependent methods that have access to strong supervision. LinEAS is modality-agnostic and we empirically find that it outperforms existing activation steering methods at mitigating and including new concepts at the output of single-step text-to-image generation models.

papers.title: Not All Language Model Features Are One-Dimensionally Linear
papers.research_question: Are some language model representations inherently multi-dimensional, and if so, how are these irreducible multi-dimensional features used in computation?
papers.core_contribution: This paper demonstrates that language models learn irreducible multi-dimensional features (e.g., circular representations for days of the week and months of the year) and provides evidence that these features are the fundamental unit of computation for modular arithmetic tasks.
papers.conclusion: Understanding multi-dimensional features is necessary for a complete mechanistic decomposition of some language model behaviors, challenging the strict one-dimensional linear representation hypothesis.
papers.key_findings:
Sparse autoencoders can automatically discover interpretable multi-dimensional features in language models, such as circular representations for days of the week and months of the year.
These circular features are irreducible according to formal separability and mixture indices, meaning they cannot be decomposed into independent or non-co-occurring lower-dimensional features.
Models like Mistral 7B and Llama 3 8B use these exact circular representations when solving modular arithmetic problems involving days and months.
Intervention experiments (subspace patching) show that the circular representations are causally involved in the model's computation for these tasks.
The circular representations respect a continuous notion of time, as shown by interventions with phrases like 'early Monday' and 'late Monday'.
papers.abstract: Recent work has proposed that language models perform computation by manipulating one-dimensional representations of concepts ("features") in activation space. In contrast, we explore whether some language model representations may be inherently multi-dimensional. We begin by developing a rigorous definition of irreducible multi-dimensional features based on whether they can be decomposed into either independent or non-co-occurring lower-dimensional features. Motivated by these definitions, we design a scalable method that uses sparse autoencoders to automatically find multi-dimensional features in GPT-2 and Mistral 7B. These auto-discovered features include strikingly interpretable examples, e.g. circular features representing days of the week and months of the year. We identify tasks where these exact circles are used to solve computational problems involving modular arithmetic in days of the week and months of the year. Next, we provide evidence that these circular features are indeed the fundamental unit of computation in these tasks with intervention experiments on Mistral 7B and Llama 3 8B, and we examine the continuity of the days of the week feature in Mistral 7B.
