papers.abstract: Logit Lens is a widely adopted method for mechanistic interpretability of transformer-based language models, enabling the analysis of how internal representations evolve across layers by projecting them into the output vocabulary space. Although applying Logit Lens to Vision Transformers (ViTs) is technically straightforward, its direct use faces limitations in capturing the richness of visual representations. Building on the work of Toker et al. (2024)~\cite{Toker2024-ve}, who introduced Diffusion Lens to visualize intermediate representations in the text encoders of text-to-image diffusion models, we demonstrate that while Diffusion Lens can effectively visualize residual stream representations in image encoders, it fails to capture the direct contributions of individual submodules. To overcome this limitation, we propose \textbf{Diffusion Steering Lens} (DSL), a novel, training-free approach that steers submodule outputs and patches subsequent indirect contributions. We validate our method through interventional studies, showing that DSL provides an intuitive and reliable interpretation of the internal processing in ViTs.

papers.title: Discovering and Steering Interpretable Concepts in Large Generative Music Models
papers.research_question: How can we discover and interpret the internal concepts learned by autoregressive music generation models, and can we use these concepts to steer generation?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces a pipeline using sparse autoencoders to discover interpretable concepts in autoregressive music models, and shows that these concepts can be used to steer generation.
papers.conclusion: The results demonstrate the feasibility and potential of using sparse autoencoders to discover interpretable concepts in large music generative models, offering a scalable path towards understanding how these models represent and generate music.
papers.key_findings:
SAEs can discover both familiar musical concepts (e.g., genres, instruments) and novel coherent patterns lacking clear theoretical description.
Later layers in the model encode more interpretable features on average, as measured by CLAP alignment with automatic labels.
Larger models (MusicGen-Large) produce features that are more distinctive by layer compared to smaller models (MusicGen-Small).
Automated labeling using Essentia classifiers and multimodal LLMs (Gemini) can label thousands of features at scale, with Essentia tags achieving higher human confidence.
A non-trivial fraction (15-35%) of discovered features can be used to steer model generations, altering outputs toward the intended concept.
papers.limitation: The analysis focuses on unconditional audio representations, not text-conditioned activations, which limits understanding of how prompts influence internal concepts.
future_direction: Extending the method to text-conditioned activations and multimodal interpretability.
Building a comprehensive understanding of how neural networks represent and generate music.
papers.abstract: The fidelity with which neural networks can now generate content such as music presents a scientific opportunity: these systems appear to have learned implicit theories of such content's structure through statistical learning alone. This offers a potentially new lens on theories of human-generated media. When internal representations align with traditional constructs (e.g. chord progressions in music), they show how such categories can emerge from statistical regularities; when they diverge, they expose limits of existing frameworks and patterns we may have overlooked but that nonetheless carry explanatory power. In this paper, focusing on music generators, we introduce a method for discovering interpretable concepts using sparse autoencoders (SAEs), extracting interpretable features from the residual stream of a transformer model. We make this approach scalable and evaluable using automated labeling and validation pipelines. Our results reveal both familiar musical concepts and coherent but uncodified patterns lacking clear counterparts in theory or language. As an extension, we show such concepts can be used to steer model generations. Beyond improving model transparency, our work provides an empirical tool for uncovering organizing principles that have eluded traditional methods of analysis and synthesis.

papers.title: Inducing Transformer's Compositional Generalization Ability via Auxiliary Sequence Prediction Tasks
papers.research_question: How can auxiliary sequence prediction tasks induce compositional generalization ability in Transformer models?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes auxiliary sequence prediction tasks to induce compositional generalization in Transformers, achieving perfect accuracy on challenging SCAN splits.
papers.conclusion: Auxiliary sequence prediction tasks can effectively induce compositional generalization in Transformers, with potential for few-shot learning and application to other datasets.
papers.key_findings:
Auxiliary sequence prediction enables Transformers to achieve 100% accuracy on SCAN MCD splits.
The method is sample-efficient, achieving 97.8% accuracy with only 5% training data.
Both auxiliary sequences are necessary for optimal performance.
Using less contextualized decoder vectors as queries improves compositional generalization.
The approach generalizes to the grounded-SCAN task.
papers.limitation:
SCAN is a synthetic dataset, so findings may not transfer to large-scale natural datasets.
Applying the method to natural language requires designing heuristics to approximate grammar.
future_direction: Using human-annotated auxiliary sequences for natural datasets.
papers.abstract: Systematic compositionality is an essential mechanism in human language, allowing the recombination of known parts to create novel expressions. However, existing neural models have been shown to lack this basic ability in learning symbolic structures. Motivated by the failure of a Transformer model on the SCAN compositionality challenge (Lake and Baroni, 2018), which requires parsing a command into actions, we propose two auxiliary sequence prediction tasks that track the progress of function and argument semantics, as additional training supervision. These automatically-generated sequences are more representative of the underlying compositional symbolic structures of the input data. During inference, the model jointly predicts the next action and the next tokens in the auxiliary sequences at each step. Experiments on the SCAN dataset show that our method encourages the Transformer to understand compositional structures of the command, improving its accuracy on multiple challenging splits from <= 10% to 100%. With only 418 (5%) training instances, our approach still achieves 97.8% accuracy on the MCD1 split. Therefore, we argue that compositionality can be induced in Transformers given minimal but proper guidance. We also show that a better result is achieved using less contextualized vectors as the attention's query, providing insights into architecture choices in achieving systematic compositionality. Finally, we show positive generalization results on the groundedSCAN task (Ruis et al., 2020). Our code is publicly available at: https://github.com/jiangycTarheel/compositional-auxseq

papers.title: Representational Homomorphism Predicts and Improves Compositional Generalization In Transformer Language Model
papers.research_question: How does homomorphism error (HE) change with model size, training data coverage, and noise injection, and how does it relate to out-of-distribution (OOD) compositional generalization? Does explicitly regularizing HE during training reduce HE and improve OOD accuracy?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces Homomorphism Error (HE), a structural metric that formalizes compositionality as approximate homomorphisms between expression spaces and model representations, and shows it predicts OOD compositional generalization and can be used as a regularizer to improve it.
papers.conclusion: Homomorphism error serves as both a diagnostic and an actionable training signal for improving compositional generalization in transformer language models.
papers.key_findings:
Homomorphism Error (HE) predicts out-of-distribution compositional generalization under noise injection, achieving R^2 = 0.73 correlation.
Model depth (number of transformer layers) has minimal effect on either HE or OOD accuracy.
Training data coverage exhibits threshold effects; models trained with only one primitive fail to generalize.
Randomly inserted noise tokens increase HE and degrade OOD accuracy.
HE-regularized training significantly reduces HE (p=1.1e-04) and yields a statistically significant improvement in OOD accuracy (p=0.023).
papers.limitation:
Experiments are conducted on synthetic data with controlled compositional structure, limiting generalizability to real-world language with ambiguity and irregular constructions.
Evaluation focuses on small Transformer models; the behavior of homomorphism error in large-scale pretrained language models remains an open question.
future_direction: Applying homomorphism error analysis to established compositional benchmarks using natural language.
Investigating how homomorphism error scales with model size and pretraining data.
Exploring compositionally-aware architecture search and training procedures.
papers.abstract: Compositional generalization-the ability to interpret novel combinations of familiar components-remains a persistent challenge for neural networks. Behavioral evaluations reveal when models fail but offer limited insight into why failures arise at the representational level. We introduce Homomorphism Error (HE), a structural metric that quantifies deviations from approximate homomorphisms between the expression algebra and a model's hidden-state space. We instantiate HE for two compositional operators in SCAN-style tasks: modifier HE for unary composition and sequence HE for binary composition, measured by learning representation-level operators that predict composed representations from their parts. Across controlled experiments with small decoder-only Transformers, HE predicts out-of-distribution (OOD) compositional generalization under noise injection, achieving R^2 = 0.73 correlation between modifier HE and OOD accuracy. Ablations show that model depth has minimal effect on either HE or OOD accuracy, training data coverage exhibits threshold effects (insufficient coverage sharply increases HE and degrades OOD performance), and randomly inserted noise tokens systematically increase HE. Finally, we test if HE-regularized training improves OOD accuracy. Experiment shows that explicitly enforcing low modifier HE during training significantly reduces modifier HE (p = 1.1x10-4) and sequence HE (p = 0.001) and yields a statistically significant improvement in OOD accuracy (p = 0.023). Together, these results indicate the potential of HE to be both a diagnostic and an actionable training signal for improving compositional generalization. Code to reproduce our experiments is open-sourced.

papers.title: Sparse Autoencoders Find Highly Interpretable Features in Language Models
papers.research_question: Can sparse autoencoders find interpretable, monosemantic features in language models by resolving superposition, and can these features be used for causal analysis and circuit discovery?
papers.core_contribution: Sparse autoencoders provide a scalable, unsupervised method to find interpretable, monosemantic features in language models, enabling precise causal analysis and circuit discovery.
papers.conclusion: Sparse autoencoders are a scalable, unsupervised approach to disentangling language model features from superposition, facilitating interpretability, circuit mapping, and targeted model editing.
papers.key_findings:
Sparse autoencoder features are more interpretable than neurons, PCA, ICA, and random directions as measured by autointerpretability scores.
Sparse autoencoder features allow more precise localization of causally important features for the IOI task than PCA, requiring fewer patches to achieve a given KL divergence.
Individual features are monosemantic (e.g., an apostrophe feature) and have predictable effects on output logits, such as suppressing the 's' token after an apostrophe.
Sparse autoencoders enable automatic circuit detection across layers, as demonstrated for a closing parenthesis feature.
The method works well on residual stream activations but has limitations for MLP layers, where many features become dead.
papers.limitation:
The autoencoders do not achieve zero reconstruction loss, indicating they fail to capture all information in the activations.
Replacing activations with reconstructions increases perplexity, showing loss of information.
The method is less robust for MLP layers, where many features become dead.
Autointerpretability has limitations, such as GPT-4 struggling with patterns centered around next or previous tokens.
future_direction: Explore other sparse autoencoder architectures and minimize change in model outputs when replacing activations.
Incorporate information about model weights or dictionary features from adjacent layers into training.
Improve feature discovery in MLP and attention layers, and generalize to other tasks and behaviors.
papers.abstract: One of the roadblocks to a better understanding of neural networks' internals is \textit{polysemanticity}, where neurons appear to activate in multiple, semantically distinct contexts. Polysemanticity prevents us from identifying concise, human-understandable explanations for what neural networks are doing internally. One hypothesised cause of polysemanticity is \textit{superposition}, where neural networks represent more features than they have neurons by assigning features to an overcomplete set of directions in activation space, rather than to individual neurons. Here, we attempt to identify those directions, using sparse autoencoders to reconstruct the internal activations of a language model. These autoencoders learn sets of sparsely activating features that are more interpretable and monosemantic than directions identified by alternative approaches, where interpretability is measured by automated methods. Moreover, we show that with our learned set of features, we can pinpoint the features that are causally responsible for counterfactual behaviour on the indirect object identification task \citep{wang2022interpretability} to a finer degree than previous decompositions. This work indicates that it is possible to resolve superposition in language models using a scalable, unsupervised method. Our method may serve as a foundation for future mechanistic interpretability work, which we hope will enable greater model transparency and steerability.

papers.title: In-Context Compositional Learning via Sparse Coding Transformer
papers.research_question: How can we reformulate the attention mechanism using sparse coding to improve Transformers' performance on in-context compositional learning tasks?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces a reformulation of the attention mechanism inspired by sparse coding, where inputs are represented as sparse combinations of learned dictionary atoms, enabling better capture and transfer of compositional rules in in-context learning tasks.
papers.conclusion: The sparse coding reformulation of attention enhances compositional learning and generalization, as demonstrated on several benchmarks, highlighting the potential of combining sparse coding principles with attention for structured reasoning.
papers.key_findings:
The proposed method outperforms standard Transformers on S-RAVEN and RAVEN datasets, achieving higher accuracy and better reconstruction quality.
Sparse coefficients lead to sharper attention patterns and prevent blurry outputs, enabling effective transfer of compositional rules.
Coefficient transfer via linear combination of context coefficients is crucial for estimating target task outputs.
The method maintains performance even when standard Transformers fail on novel compositional rules.
When integrated into Llama-7B, the method improves performance on commonsense reasoning benchmarks with few added parameters.
papers.limitation: The approach has only been tested on relatively small-scale tasks; its application to large pre-trained models remains unexplored.
future_direction: Integrating the linear combination of attention maps into pre-trained models to enhance compositional learning.
Exploring application to other benchmarks such as translation, summarization, or image generation tasks.
papers.abstract: Transformer architectures have achieved remarkable success across language, vision, and multimodal tasks, and there is growing demand for them to address in-context compositional learning tasks. In these tasks, models solve the target problems by inferring compositional rules from context examples, which are composed of basic components structured by underlying rules. However, some of these tasks remain challenging for Transformers, which are not inherently designed to handle compositional tasks and offer limited structural inductive bias. In this work, inspired by the principle of sparse coding, we propose a reformulation of the attention to enhance its capability for compositional tasks. In sparse coding, data are represented as sparse combinations of dictionary atoms with coefficients that capture their compositional rules. Specifically, we reinterpret the attention block as a mapping of inputs into outputs through projections onto two sets of learned dictionary atoms: an encoding dictionary and a decoding dictionary. The encoding dictionary decomposes the input into a set of coefficients, which represent the compositional structure of the input. To enhance structured representations, we impose sparsity on these coefficients. The sparse coefficients are then used to linearly combine the decoding dictionary atoms to generate the output. Furthermore, to assist compositional generalization tasks, we propose estimating the coefficients of the target problem as a linear combination of the coefficients obtained from the context examples. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach on the S-RAVEN and RAVEN datasets. For certain compositional generalization tasks, our method maintains performance even when standard Transformers fail, owing to its ability to learn and apply compositional rules.

papers.title: Counterfactuals uncover the modular structure of deep generative models
papers.research_question: How can we uncover the modular structure of deep generative models in an unsupervised way using counterfactual manipulations?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces a causal framework for unsupervised discovery of modular structure in deep generative models using counterfactuals, and demonstrates that such structure exists in various models, enabling targeted interventions.
papers.conclusion: Counterfactuals can uncover modular structure in deep generative models, enabling applications such as computationally efficient style transfer and automated assessment of robustness to contextual changes in pattern recognition systems.
papers.key_findings:
Generative models like BigGAN, β-VAE, DCGAN, and BEGAN exhibit interpretable modules of internal variables (channels) that encode different features (e.g., background, face, hair in faces; object and background in ImageNet).
These modules can be used for targeted interventions, such as hybridizing images by swapping modules between two samples, effectively transferring features.
The modular structure allows for faithful counterfactual manipulations that stay within the data manifold, enabling applications like style transfer.
Clustering of influence maps (derived from counterfactual effects) using NMF yields stable and interpretable modules, outperforming k-means.
The approach scales to high-resolution models (BigGAN) and complex datasets (ImageNet), producing high-quality counterfactual images.
papers.limitation:
Our approach is limited to feed-forward architectures and requires the generative model to be injective (to define counterfactuals).
We have not investigated the relationship between intrinsic and extrinsic disentanglement.
future_direction: Investigate the relationship between intrinsic and extrinsic disentanglement.
Applications to style transfer and robustness assessment of classifiers.
papers.abstract: Deep generative models can emulate the perceptual properties of complex image datasets, providing a latent representation of the data. However, manipulating such representation to perform meaningful and controllable transformations in the data space remains challenging without some form of supervision. While previous work has focused on exploiting statistical independence to disentangle latent factors, we argue that such requirement is too restrictive and propose instead a non-statistical framework that relies on counterfactual manipulations to uncover a modular structure of the network composed of disentangled groups of internal variables. Experiments with a variety of generative models trained on complex image datasets show the obtained modules can be used to design targeted interventions. This opens the way to applications such as computationally efficient style transfer and the automated assessment of robustness to contextual changes in pattern recognition systems.

papers.title: How Transformers Learn Causal Structure with Gradient Descent
papers.research_question: How do transformers learn causal structure with gradient descent?
papers.core_contribution: Proves that gradient descent on a two-layer transformer learns causal structure by encoding the latent causal graph in the first attention layer, with the gradient of the attention matrix encoding mutual information between tokens.
papers.conclusion: Transformers learn causal structure by encoding the causal graph in the first attention layer through gradient descent, with the gradient encoding mutual information.
papers.key_findings:
Gradient descent on a two-layer transformer learns to encode the latent causal graph in the first attention layer.
The gradient of the attention matrix encodes mutual information between tokens, and the largest entries correspond to edges in the causal graph.
For in-context Markov chains, transformers learn an induction head.
Empirically, transformers trained on the task recover a wide variety of causal structures.
For multiple parents, transformers can distribute the causal graph across multiple attention heads.
papers.abstract: The incredible success of transformers on sequence modeling tasks can be largely attributed to the self-attention mechanism, which allows information to be transferred between different parts of a sequence. Self-attention allows transformers to encode causal structure which makes them particularly suitable for sequence modeling. However, the process by which transformers learn such causal structure via gradient-based training algorithms remains poorly understood. To better understand this process, we introduce an in-context learning task that requires learning latent causal structure. We prove that gradient descent on a simplified two-layer transformer learns to solve this task by encoding the latent causal graph in the first attention layer. The key insight of our proof is that the gradient of the attention matrix encodes the mutual information between tokens. As a consequence of the data processing inequality, the largest entries of this gradient correspond to edges in the latent causal graph. As a special case, when the sequences are generated from in-context Markov chains, we prove that transformers learn an induction head (Olsson et al., 2022). We confirm our theoretical findings by showing that transformers trained on our in-context learning task are able to recover a wide variety of causal structures.

papers.title: When Can Transformers Ground and Compose: Insights from Compositional Generalization Benchmarks
papers.research_question: When and how can transformer models ground language to a visual world and generalize compositionally?
papers.core_contribution: Simple transformer-based models (GroCoT) can achieve strong compositional generalization on grounded navigation tasks, and a simplified task (RefEx) reveals that even a single attention layer can ground and compose attributes, with its computations being fully interpretable.
papers.conclusion: Transformers are capable of grounded compositional generalization, with the primary difficulty in existing benchmarks being target identification, and a simplified task (RefEx) allows for a complete interpretation of the model's grounding and compositional reasoning.
papers.key_findings:
GroCoT outperforms specialized architectures on ReaSCAN and GSRR benchmarks.
The main challenge in ReaSCAN is target identification, not navigation sequence generation.
The C2 test split in ReaSCAN is unfair; transformers can generalize to deeper structures when trained fairly.
A single self-attention layer with a single head can solve the RefEx task and generalize to novel compositions of object attributes.
The computations of the attention-only transformer on RefEx can be mathematically constructed, providing a complete interpretation of how grounding and composition occur.
papers.abstract: Humans can reason compositionally whilst grounding language utterances to the real world. Recent benchmarks like ReaSCAN use navigation tasks grounded in a grid world to assess whether neural models exhibit similar capabilities. In this work, we present a simple transformer-based model that outperforms specialized architectures on ReaSCAN and a modified version of gSCAN. On analyzing the task, we find that identifying the target location in the grid world is the main challenge for the models. Furthermore, we show that a particular split in ReaSCAN, which tests depth generalization, is unfair. On an amended version of this split, we show that transformers can generalize to deeper input structures. Finally, we design a simpler grounded compositional generalization task, RefEx, to investigate how transformers reason compositionally. We show that a single self-attention layer with a single head generalizes to novel combinations of object attributes. Moreover, we derive a precise mathematical construction of the transformer's computations from the learned network. Overall, we provide valuable insights about the grounded compositional generalization task and the behaviour of transformers on it, which would be useful for researchers working in this area.

papers.title: Decomposing MLP Activations into Interpretable Features via Semi-Nonnegative Matrix Factorization
papers.research_question: How can we find interpretable features in large language models by decomposing MLP activations using semi-nonnegative matrix factorization?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces SNMF for decomposing MLP activations into interpretable features, outperforming SAEs and supervised baselines in causal steering, and reveals hierarchical structure in MLP activation space.
papers.conclusion: SNMF is a simple and effective tool for identifying interpretable features and dissecting concept representations in LLMs.
papers.key_findings:
SNMF-derived features outperform SAEs and a supervised baseline (difference-in-means) on causal steering.
SNMF features align with human-interpretable concepts and show good concept detection.
Recursive SNMF reveals hierarchical merging of features, e.g., fine-grained concepts into high-level ones.
Specific neuron combinations are reused across semantically-related features.
MLP features are compositional and exhibit a parts-based decomposition.
papers.limitation: A minority of MLP features receive negative scores, indicating they respond more strongly to neutral contexts, possibly reflecting sensitivity to noise or layer-specific biases.
future_direction: Optimizations for SNMF initialization and training
papers.abstract: A central goal for mechanistic interpretability has been to identify the right units of analysis in large language models (LLMs) that causally explain their outputs. While early work focused on individual neurons, evidence that neurons often encode multiple concepts has motivated a shift toward analyzing directions in activation space. A key question is how to find directions that capture interpretable features in an unsupervised manner. Current methods rely on dictionary learning with sparse autoencoders (SAEs), commonly trained over residual stream activations to learn directions from scratch. However, SAEs often struggle in causal evaluations and lack intrinsic interpretability, as their learning is not explicitly tied to the computations of the model. Here, we tackle these limitations by directly decomposing MLP activations with semi-nonnegative matrix factorization (SNMF), such that the learned features are (a) sparse linear combinations of co-activated neurons, and (b) mapped to their activating inputs, making them directly interpretable. Experiments on Llama 3.1, Gemma 2 and GPT-2 show that SNMF derived features outperform SAEs and a strong supervised baseline (difference-in-means) on causal steering, while aligning with human-interpretable concepts. Further analysis reveals that specific neuron combinations are reused across semantically-related features, exposing a hierarchical structure in the MLP's activation space. Together, these results position SNMF as a simple and effective tool for identifying interpretable features and dissecting concept representations in LLMs.

papers.title: Unlocking Out-of-Distribution Generalization in Transformers via Recursive Latent Space Reasoning
papers.research_question: What are the architectural mechanisms and inductive biases needed for robust OOD algorithmic generalization in Transformers?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces four architectural mechanisms (input-adaptive recurrence, algorithmic supervision, discrete latent space, error correction) that enable Transformers to achieve robust out-of-distribution generalization on a mathematical reasoning task, and provides mechanistic interpretability analysis of the learned circuits.
papers.conclusion: The paper presents an architectural approach for native latent-space reasoning in Transformer networks, demonstrating robust algorithmic generalization capabilities and providing insights through mechanistic interpretability.
papers.key_findings:
Standard chain-of-thought training enables limited out-of-distribution generalization but performance degrades rapidly beyond the training distribution.
The proposed four mechanisms (recurrence, algorithmic supervision, discretization, error correction) enable perfect generalization to inputs several times larger than those seen during training.
Mechanistic interpretability reveals that the model learns circuits for variable copying in the first attention layer and value copying in the second attention layer.
The second layer MLP performs modular addition in the frequency domain, amplifying diagonal frequency components that encode the sum.
The discrete latent space anchors representations to a common space, preventing representational shift and facilitating scaling.
papers.limitation: The model does not perform self-correction when trained on perfect data.
future_direction: Training the model with corrupted data to enable self-correction
papers.abstract: Systematic, compositional generalization beyond the training distribution remains a core challenge in machine learning -- and a critical bottleneck for the emergent reasoning abilities of modern language models. This work investigates out-of-distribution (OOD) generalization in Transformer networks using a GSM8K-style modular arithmetic on computational graphs task as a testbed. We introduce and explore a set of four architectural mechanisms aimed at enhancing OOD generalization: (i) input-adaptive recurrence; (ii) algorithmic supervision; (iii) anchored latent representations via a discrete bottleneck; and (iv) an explicit error-correction mechanism. Collectively, these mechanisms yield an architectural approach for native and scalable latent space reasoning in Transformer networks with robust algorithmic generalization capabilities. We complement these empirical results with a detailed mechanistic interpretability analysis that reveals how these mechanisms give rise to robust OOD generalization abilities.

papers.title: Characterizing Intrinsic Compositionality in Transformers with Tree Projections
papers.research_question: Does the transformer learn a tree-like computation when trained on language data, and how can we measure its tree-structuredness?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces an unsupervised, parameter-free method to functionally project transformers into tree-structured networks, showing that transformers become more tree-like during training and that tree-structuredness predicts compositional generalization.
papers.conclusion: Overall, our results suggest that making further progress on human-like compositional generalization might require inductive biases that encourage the emergence of latent tree-like structure.
papers.key_findings:
Transformers become more tree-like over training on sequence transduction tasks.
Tree projections sometimes align with gold syntax.
Induced trees reflect contextual dependence structure.
Tree-structuredness correlates better with compositional generalization than in-domain accuracy.
Self-supervised training does not lead to tree-like computation in low data regimes.
papers.abstract: When trained on language data, do transformers learn some arbitrary computation that utilizes the full capacity of the architecture or do they learn a simpler, tree-like computation, hypothesized to underlie compositional meaning systems like human languages? There is an apparent tension between compositional accounts of human language understanding, which are based on a restricted bottom-up computational process, and the enormous success of neural models like transformers, which can route information arbitrarily between different parts of their input. One possibility is that these models, while extremely flexible in principle, in practice learn to interpret language hierarchically, ultimately building sentence representations close to those predictable by a bottom-up, tree-structured model. To evaluate this possibility, we describe an unsupervised and parameter-free method to \emph{functionally project} the behavior of any transformer into the space of tree-structured networks. Given an input sentence, we produce a binary tree that approximates the transformer's representation-building process and a score that captures how "tree-like" the transformer's behavior is on the input. While calculation of this score does not require training any additional models, it provably upper-bounds the fit between a transformer and any tree-structured approximation. Using this method, we show that transformers for three different tasks become more tree-like over the course of training, in some cases unsupervisedly recovering the same trees as supervised parsers. These trees, in turn, are predictive of model behavior, with more tree-like models generalizing better on tests of compositional generalization.

papers.title: The Physics of Data and Tasks: Theories of Locality and Compositionality in Deep Learning
papers.research_question: What is the latent structure of learnable data, and how do neural networks encode and exploit it to achieve generalization?
papers.core_contribution: The thesis develops a theoretical framework showing that locality and compositionality in data and tasks enable deep networks to overcome the curse of dimensionality, and demonstrates that diffusion models learn hierarchical grammars and that task arithmetic in pre-trained models is enabled by weight disentanglement.
papers.conclusion: This thesis proposes that deep learning is effective because it operates on a cascade of compositional structures, from local features to hierarchical representations and modular organization of knowledge in weight space.
papers.key_findings:
Locality in CNNs allows them to overcome the curse of dimensionality by adapting to the spatial scale of the target function.
Diffusion models exhibit a phase transition during generation, revealing the hierarchical compositionality of natural data.
The sample complexity for learning hierarchical grammars scales polynomially with dimension, explaining how diffusion models avoid the curse of dimensionality.
Weight disentanglement in pre-trained models enables task arithmetic and model editing.
Hierarchical learning requires feature learning, not just kernel methods.
papers.limitation: The Random Hierarchy Model, while rich, is still a simplification of natural data.
future_direction: Extending the theory to other generative models (e.g., autoregressive models)
Understanding the emergence of weight disentanglement during pre-training
Scaling laws for hierarchical learning
papers.abstract: Deep neural networks have achieved remarkable success, yet our understanding of how they learn remains limited. These models can learn high-dimensional tasks, which is generally statistically intractable due to the curse of dimensionality. This apparent paradox suggests that learnable data must have an underlying latent structure. What is the nature of this structure? How do neural networks encode and exploit it, and how does it quantitatively impact performance - for instance, how does generalization improve with the number of training examples? This thesis addresses these questions by studying the roles of locality and compositionality in data, tasks, and deep learning representations. We begin by analyzing convolutional neural networks in the limit of infinite width, where the learning dynamics simplifies and becomes analytically tractable. Using tools from statistical physics and learning theory, we characterize their generalization abilities and show that they can overcome the curse of dimensionality if the target function is local by adapting to its spatial scale. We then turn to more complex structures in which features are composed hierarchically, with elements at larger scales built from sub-features at smaller ones. We model such data using simple probabilistic context-free grammars - tree-like graphical models used to describe data such as language and images. Within this framework, we study how diffusion-based generative models compose new data by assembling features learned from examples. This theory of composition predicts a phase transition in the generative process, which we confirm empirically in both image and language modalities, providing support for the compositional structure of natural data. We further demonstrate that the sample complexity for learning these grammars scales polynomially with data dimension, providing a mechanism by which diffusion models avoid the curse of dimensionality by learning to hierarchically compose new data. These results offer a theoretical grounding for how generative models learn to generalize, and ultimately, become creative. Finally, we shift our analysis from the structure of data in the input space to the structure of tasks in the model's parameter space. Here, we investigate a novel form of compositionality, where tasks and skills themselves can be composed. In particular, we empirically demonstrate that distinct directions in the weight space of large pre-trained models are associated with localized, semantic task-specific areas in function space, and how this modular structure enables task arithmetic and model editing at scale.

papers.title: Transformers learn factored representations
papers.research_question: Do transformers learn to factor their world into parts from next-token prediction, and why would they have an inductive bias for factored representations?
papers.core_contribution: Transformers learn to factor their world into parts, representing each factor in orthogonal subspaces of the residual stream, and show an inductive bias toward factored representations even when it is lossy.
papers.conclusion: Transformers decompose the world into parts and represent them in orthogonal subspaces due to an inductive bias from next-token prediction, suggesting interpretable low-dimensional structure may persist in models trained on complex data.
papers.key_findings:
Transformers learn factored representations in orthogonal subspaces when data has conditionally independent factors.
The dimensionality of activations collapses to the linearly growing factored prediction, not the exponentially growing joint representation.
Factor subspaces become approximately orthogonal over training, as measured by subspace overlap and dimensionality additivity.
Factoring begins at the token embedding layer, with the embedding matrix developing low-rank structure corresponding to factor subspaces.
Transformers exhibit an inductive bias toward factored representations, learning them early even when data is not perfectly factorable, sacrificing fidelity for dimensional efficiency.
papers.limitation: Experiments are conducted on synthetic data with known latent structure, which may not fully capture real-world complexity.
future_direction: Investigate whether differences in factorization behavior between transformers, RNNs, and LSTMs are due to training dynamics or inductive bias.
papers.abstract: Transformers pretrained via next token prediction learn to factor their world into parts, representing these factors in orthogonal subspaces of the residual stream. We formalize two representational hypotheses: (1) a representation in the product space of all factors, whose dimension grows exponentially with the number of parts, or (2) a factored representation in orthogonal subspaces, whose dimension grows linearly. The factored representation is lossless when factors are conditionally independent, but sacrifices predictive fidelity otherwise, creating a tradeoff between dimensional efficiency and accuracy. We derive precise predictions about the geometric structure of activations for each, including the number of subspaces, their dimensionality, and the arrangement of context embeddings within them. We test between these hypotheses on transformers trained on synthetic processes with known latent structure. Models learn factored representations when factors are conditionally independent, and continue to favor them early in training even when noise or hidden dependencies undermine conditional independence, reflecting an inductive bias toward factoring at the cost of fidelity. This provides a principled explanation for why transformers decompose the world into parts, and suggests that interpretable low dimensional structure may persist even in models trained on complex data.

papers.title: Interpretable Steering of Large Language Models with Feature Guided Activation Additions
papers.research_question: How can we improve the precision and interpretability of activation steering in large language models by leveraging sparse autoencoder features and optimization techniques?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces Feature Guided Activation Additions (FGAA), a novel activation steering method that uses sparse autoencoder features and optimization to construct precise, interpretable steering vectors, improving steering effectiveness and output coherence compared to existing methods.
papers.conclusion: FGAA represents a significant step forward in controlled text generation, offering both theoretical insights into activation patterns and practical advances in steering methodology, while highlighting the trade-off between steering strength and capability preservation.
papers.key_findings:
FGAA outperforms existing activation steering methods (CAA, SAE, SAE-TS) on most steering tasks, especially for the Gemma-2-2B model.
FGAA provides more interpretable steering by operating in the SAE feature space and allowing explicit control over which features are steered.
There is a trade-off between steering strength and preservation of model capabilities: all steering methods degrade model performance (perplexity and benchmark accuracy) at high steering scales.
Negative features in steering vectors tend to degrade steering performance, so FGAA focuses on positive features.
The effectiveness of FGAA varies with model size, showing different performance patterns between Gemma-2-2B and Gemma-2-9B.
papers.limitation:
Relies heavily on the quality of feature extraction by the underlying Sparse Autoencoder (SAE).
Optimal selection of n1 and n2 parameters is task-dependent, making universal guidelines challenging.
Developing metrics to evaluate the effectiveness of feature filtering methods is challenging due to the qualitative nature of interpreting features.
future_direction: Investigating how SAE width and quality of SAE features affects steering performance with FGAA.
Exploring techniques to minimize capability degradation at higher steering scales while maintaining steering effectiveness.
Applying FGAA to safety tasks such as controlling sycophancy, hallucination, and refusal in RLHF models and reducing social biases.
papers.abstract: Effective and reliable control over large language model (LLM) behavior is a significant challenge. While activation steering methods, which add steering vectors to a model's hidden states, are a promising approach, existing techniques often lack precision and interpretability in how they influence model outputs. We introduce Feature Guided Activation Additions (FGAA), a novel activation steering method that leverages insights from Contrastive Activation Addition (CAA) and Sparse Autoencoder-Targeted Steering (SAE-TS). By operating in the latent space of a Sparse Autoencoder (SAE) and employing optimization techniques to select desired SAE features, FGAA constructs precise steering vectors that provide better steering effects while maintaining coherence of steered model outputs. In this regard, evaluations on Gemma-2-2B and Gemma-2-9B models across various steering tasks demonstrate that FGAA outperforms existing steering methods of CAA, SAE decoder steering, and SAE-TS. Our results also highlight important trade-offs between steering scale and general model capabilities that are consistent across all tested steering methods.

papers.title: Causal Interpretation of Sparse Autoencoder Features in Vision
papers.research_question: How to causally interpret sparse autoencoder features in vision transformers by identifying the image patches that drive activations, rather than relying on correlational activation maps?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes Causal Feature Explanation (CaFE), which uses effective receptive field attribution to provide causal explanations for SAE features in vision transformers, demonstrating improved faithfulness over activation-based methods.
papers.conclusion: CaFE provides more faithful and semantically precise interpretations of visual features by using causal ERF-based explanations, preventing misinterpretation from activation-based methods.
papers.key_findings:
CaFE with ERF attribution more accurately identifies causal image patches for SAE feature activations compared to naive activation maps.
Non-localized SAE features exist, especially in higher layers, where activations scatter across the image.
ERF maps reveal hidden context dependencies, such as features requiring co-occurrence of multiple objects.
Insertion tests show that CaFE with AttnLRP achieves higher causal recovery rates than activation-based baselines.
The frequency of non-local features increases with transformer layer depth, peaking in later layers.
papers.limitation:
Computing the ERF for each feature requires both forward and backward passes, which may be costly for very deep SAEs.
Manual annotation of non-local features is inherently subjective; devising scalable, automated criteria remains future work.
future_direction: Devising scalable, automated criteria for identifying non-local features
Extending CaFE with ERF-based attribution to text modalities
papers.abstract: Understanding what sparse auto-encoder (SAE) features in vision transformers truly represent is usually done by inspecting the patches where a feature's activation is highest. However, self-attention mixes information across the entire image, so an activated patch often co-occurs with-but does not cause-the feature's firing. We propose Causal Feature Explanation (CaFE), which leverages Effective Receptive Field (ERF). We consider each activation of an SAE feature to be a target and apply input-attribution methods to identify the image patches that causally drive that activation. Across CLIP-ViT features, ERF maps frequently diverge from naive activation maps, revealing hidden context dependencies (e.g., a "roaring face" feature that requires the co-occurrence of eyes and nose, rather than merely an open mouth). Patch insertion tests confirm that CaFE more effectively recovers or suppresses feature activations than activation-ranked patches. Our results show that CaFE yields more faithful and semantically precise explanations of vision-SAE features, highlighting the risk of misinterpretation when relying solely on activation location.

papers.title: One-Step is Enough: Sparse Autoencoders for Text-to-Image Diffusion Models
papers.research_question: Can sparse autoencoders learn interpretable features for text-to-image diffusion models, and do these features generalize across different denoising steps and model architectures?
papers.core_contribution: SAEs can learn interpretable features from one-step text-to-image diffusion models that generalize across steps and architectures, enabling causal intervention and revealing block specialization.
papers.conclusion: SAEs are a promising approach for understanding and manipulating the internal mechanisms of text-to-image diffusion models, and one-step training is sufficient for learning features that generalize to multi-step models.
papers.key_findings:
SAEs trained on one-step SDXL Turbo generalize to 4-step SDXL Turbo and multi-step SDXL base model without additional training.
The learned features are interpretable and causally influence the image generation process.
Transformer blocks specialize into roles: up.0.0 for details, up.0.1 for style, and down.2.1 for composition.
RIEBench shows SAE features allow fine-grained image editing with fewer features compared to neuron interventions.
One-step training is sufficient for learning meaningful features applicable to multi-step diffusion models.
papers.limitation: The change pose task is hard to achieve with the current RIEBench setup.
future_direction: Improving feature selection strategies for delete interventions
Extending SAEs to other diffusion models
Using learned features for advanced image editing and control
papers.abstract: For large language models (LLMs), sparse autoencoders (SAEs) have been shown to decompose intermediate representations that often are not interpretable directly into sparse sums of interpretable features, facilitating better control and subsequent analysis. However, similar analyses and approaches have been lacking for text-to-image models. We investigate the possibility of using SAEs to learn interpretable features for SDXL Turbo, a few-step text-to-image diffusion model. To this end, we train SAEs on the updates performed by transformer blocks within SDXL Turbo's denoising U-net in its 1-step setting. Interestingly, we find that they generalize to 4-step SDXL Turbo and even to the multi-step SDXL base model (i.e., a different model) without additional training. In addition, we show that their learned features are interpretable, causally influence the generation process, and reveal specialization among the blocks. We do so by creating RIEBench, a representation-based image editing benchmark, for editing images while they are generated by turning on and off individual SAE features. This allows us to track which transformer blocks' features are the most impactful depending on the edit category. Our work is the first investigation of SAEs for interpretability in text-to-image diffusion models and our results establish SAEs as a promising approach for understanding and manipulating the internal mechanisms of text-to-image models.

papers.title: Interpreting Large Text-to-Image Diffusion Models with Dictionary Learning
papers.research_question: How can sparse dictionary learning methods (Sparse Autoencoders and Inference-Time Decomposition of Activations) be scaled and applied to interpret and control large text-to-image diffusion models?
papers.core_contribution: This work successfully scales Sparse Autoencoders (SAEs) and Inference-Time Decomposition of Activations (ITDA) to a large text-to-image diffusion model (FLUX.1), demonstrating they can decompose residual stream activations into interpretable features and enable targeted steering of image generation.
papers.conclusion: Sparse Autoencoders and Inference-Time Decomposition of Activations are effective methods for interpreting and steering large text-to-image diffusion models, with SAE features being particularly suitable for manipulating concrete semantic concepts in generated images.
papers.key_findings:
SAEs accurately reconstruct residual stream embeddings and outperform MLP neurons on automated interpretability metrics.
ITDA achieves comparable interpretability to SAEs but tends to encode more abstract visual attributes (colors, textures) while SAE features capture more concrete objects.
Steering image generation via SAE feature activation addition is effective but constrained, requiring the initial prompt to be semantically related to the steered feature.
The residual stream activations in FLUX.1 are highly anisotropic, necessitating PCA whitening for effective SAE training to avoid a high proportion of dead features.
ITDA generally achieves superior reconstruction performance compared to SAEs at similar dictionary sizes.
papers.limitation:
Automated interpretability (autointerp) metrics do not distinguish between abstract visual properties and manipulable semantic concepts, a qualitative difference observed between ITDA and SAE features.
Steering with SAE features is constrained and only effective when the initial image prompt is semantically related to the feature being added.
The autointerp pipeline may have biases, such as picking up on simple image characteristics like color rather than the intended semantic feature.
future_direction: Applying SAEs to vision tasks like classification, segmentation, and depth estimation (sparse probing).
Adapting the SAE encoder architecture to incorporate spatial inductive bias (e.g., convolutional layers) for image data.
Improving steering techniques, potentially by making the process more similar to finetuning or otherwise more aware of steering effects.
Investigating shared features between the text and image streams of the multimodal DiT architecture.
Comparing the two FLUX.1 variants (Dev and Schnell) using methods like crosscoders to find corresponding or unique features.
Investigating biases specific to the automated interpretability pipeline.
papers.abstract: Sparse autoencoders are a promising new approach for decomposing language model activations for interpretation and control. They have been applied successfully to vision transformer image encoders and to small-scale diffusion models. Inference-Time Decomposition of Activations (ITDA) is a recently proposed variant of dictionary learning that takes the dictionary to be a set of data points from the activation distribution and reconstructs them with gradient pursuit. We apply Sparse Autoencoders (SAEs) and ITDA to a large text-to-image diffusion model, Flux 1, and consider the interpretability of embeddings of both by introducing a visual automated interpretation pipeline. We find that SAEs accurately reconstruct residual stream embeddings and beat MLP neurons on interpretability. We are able to use SAE features to steer image generation through activation addition. We find that ITDA has comparable interpretability to SAEs.

papers.title: Unlocking Compositional Generalization in Pre-trained Models Using Intermediate Representations
papers.research_question: How can intermediate representations be designed to improve compositional generalization in pre-trained seq2seq models?
papers.core_contribution: Intermediate representations designed to increase structural correspondence with natural language significantly improve compositional generalization in pre-trained seq2seq models, and these representations synergize with pre-training.
papers.conclusion: Intermediate representations are a simple yet effective strategy for improving compositional generalization in pre-trained seq2seq models, and they work synergistically with pre-training.
papers.key_findings:
Reversible intermediate representations (RIR) that group conjuncts, shorten relations, and add brackets improve compositional generalization on CFQ and SCAN.
Lossy intermediate representations (LIR) that anonymize entities and variables further improve performance when combined with RIR, especially on text-to-SQL datasets.
The benefits of intermediate representations are synergistic with pre-training; they yield larger gains when applied to pre-trained models than when applied to models without pre-training.
The best combinations of intermediate representations and pre-trained models achieve state-of-the-art results on CFQ and text-to-SQL template splits.
Intermediate representations maintain performance on i.i.d. splits while providing large gains on compositional splits.
papers.limitation: Designing intermediate representations requires customization for each new formalism, which involves manual work.
papers.abstract: Sequence-to-sequence (seq2seq) models are prevalent in semantic parsing, but have been found to struggle at out-of-distribution compositional generalization. While specialized model architectures and pre-training of seq2seq models have been proposed to address this issue, the former often comes at the cost of generality and the latter only shows limited success. In this paper, we study the impact of intermediate representations on compositional generalization in pre-trained seq2seq models, without changing the model architecture at all, and identify key aspects for designing effective representations. Instead of training to directly map natural language to an executable form, we map to a reversible or lossy intermediate representation that has stronger structural correspondence with natural language. The combination of our proposed intermediate representations and pre-trained models is surprisingly effective, where the best combinations obtain a new state-of-the-art on CFQ (+14.8 accuracy points) and on the template-splits of three text-to-SQL datasets (+15.0 to +19.4 accuracy points). This work highlights that intermediate representations provide an important and potentially overlooked degree of freedom for improving the compositional generalization abilities of pre-trained seq2seq models.

papers.title: Attention as a Hypernetwork
papers.research_question: What mechanisms underlie compositional generalization in transformers? The paper investigates whether multi-head attention can be viewed as a hypernetwork and if this perspective explains compositional generalization.
papers.core_contribution: The paper reformulates multi-head attention as a hypernetwork, showing that attention scores across heads form a latent code that specifies operations and is reused for compositional generalization. Introducing a nonlinear value network (HYLA) improves compositional generalization.
papers.conclusion: The hypernetwork perspective provides a useful framework for understanding compositional generalization in transformers, and strengthening this mechanism via a nonlinear value network (HYLA) improves compositional generalization on abstract reasoning tasks.
papers.key_findings:
Multi-head attention can be equivalently expressed as a linear hypernetwork that configures key-query specific computations via a latent code formed by attention scores across heads.
The latent code is predictive of the subtasks the network performs and shows structured clusters corresponding to task components (e.g., fuzzy logic terms or SRAVEN rules).
Scaling model size and data enables compositional generalization on abstract reasoning tasks like SRAVEN.
Modifying attention to have a nonlinear value network (HYLA) improves compositional generalization compared to standard softmax and linear attention.
Ablating the hypernetwork mechanism (e.g., using a single head) hurts compositional generalization, supporting the hypernetwork perspective.
papers.limitation: The analysis is limited to models trained from scratch, and it is unclear if large pretrained models exhibit similar latent code structure.
future_direction: Investigating whether large pretrained models form a similarly structured latent code.
Exploring other levels of granularity for the hypernetwork parameterization and different pooling operators in multi-head attention.
Connecting the hypernetwork perspective to attention-based graph neural networks.
papers.abstract: Transformers can under some circumstances generalize to novel problem instances whose constituent parts might have been encountered during training, but whose compositions have not. What mechanisms underlie this ability for compositional generalization? By reformulating multi-head attention as a hypernetwork, we reveal that a composable, low-dimensional latent code specifies key-query specific operations. We find empirically that this latent code is predictive of the subtasks the network performs on unseen task compositions, revealing that latent codes acquired during training are reused to solve unseen problem instances. To further examine the hypothesis that the intrinsic hypernetwork of multi-head attention supports compositional generalization, we ablate whether making the hypernetwork-generated linear value network nonlinear strengthens compositionality. We find that this modification improves compositional generalization on abstract reasoning tasks. In particular, we introduce a symbolic version of the Raven's Progressive Matrices human intelligence test, which gives us precise control over the problem compositions encountered during training and evaluation. We demonstrate on this task how scaling model size and data enables compositional generalization in transformers and gives rise to a functionally structured latent space.

papers.title: Interpreting Attention Layer Outputs with Sparse Autoencoders
papers.research_question: Can Sparse Autoencoders be applied to attention layer outputs to obtain interpretable features, and how can this tool be used to better understand attention mechanisms and circuits in transformers?
papers.core_contribution: The paper demonstrates that Sparse Autoencoders can decompose attention layer outputs into sparse, interpretable features, enabling deeper analysis of attention mechanisms and circuits in transformers.
papers.conclusion: Attention Output SAEs are a valuable tool for mechanistic interpretability, allowing for detailed analysis of attention layers and circuits, and should be adopted by the community.
papers.key_findings:
SAEs applied to attention layer outputs yield sparse and interpretable features, with families such as long-range context, short-range context, and induction features.
In GPT-2 Small, at least 90% of attention heads are polysemantic, performing multiple unrelated tasks.
Induction heads can be specialized, with some performing long-prefix induction and others short-prefix induction.
Attention Output SAEs can identify causally relevant features in circuits like the Indirect Object Identification circuit, providing deeper semantic understanding.
The Recursive Direct Feature Attribution (RDFA) technique enables tracing feature contributions through the model.
papers.limitation: The method for interpreting attention heads by looking at the top 10 SAE features may not capture the full role of the head and may miss behaviors that rely on multiple heads (attention head superposition).
papers.abstract: Decomposing model activations into interpretable components is a key open problem in mechanistic interpretability. Sparse autoencoders (SAEs) are a popular method for decomposing the internal activations of trained transformers into sparse, interpretable features, and have been applied to MLP layers and the residual stream. In this work we train SAEs on attention layer outputs and show that also here SAEs find a sparse, interpretable decomposition. We demonstrate this on transformers from several model families and up to 2B parameters. We perform a qualitative study of the features computed by attention layers, and find multiple families: long-range context, short-range context and induction features. We qualitatively study the role of every head in GPT-2 Small, and estimate that at least 90% of the heads are polysemantic, i.e. have multiple unrelated roles. Further, we show that Sparse Autoencoders are a useful tool that enable researchers to explain model behavior in greater detail than prior work. For example, we explore the mystery of why models have so many seemingly redundant induction heads, use SAEs to motivate the hypothesis that some are long-prefix whereas others are short-prefix, and confirm this with more rigorous analysis. We use our SAEs to analyze the computation performed by the Indirect Object Identification circuit (Wang et al.), validating that the SAEs find causally meaningful intermediate variables, and deepening our understanding of the semantics of the circuit. We open-source the trained SAEs and a tool for exploring arbitrary prompts through the lens of Attention Output SAEs.

papers.title: Surgical Activation Steering via Generative Causal Mediation
papers.research_question: Where should we intervene in a language model (LM) to localize and control behaviors that are diffused across many tokens of a long-form response?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces Generative Causal Mediation (GCM), a method for selecting attention heads that are causal mediators of a target concept using contrastive long-form responses, enabling effective localization and steering of diffuse behaviors.
papers.conclusion: GCM provides an effective approach for localizing from and controlling the long-form responses of LMs.
papers.key_findings:
GCM successfully localizes concepts expressed in long-form responses and outperforms correlational probe-based baselines when steering with a sparse set of attention heads.
GCM variants (activation patching, attribution patching, attention head knockouts) provide effective strategies for concept localization.
Steering success depends on hyperparameters like the steering factor (α) and the percentage of heads intervened on (k).
Representation Fine-Tuning (ReFT) is an effective supervised steering method when combined with GCM localization.
papers.limitation:
Activation patching is computationally expensive, scaling linearly with the number of neurons.
Attribution patching is a linear approximation that may not be perfect, especially at the first and last layers.
future_direction: Extending GCM to other model components beyond attention heads.
Applying GCM to a broader range of tasks and behaviors.
papers.abstract: Where should we intervene in a language model (LM) to control behaviors that are diffused across many tokens of a long-form response? We introduce Generative Causal Mediation (GCM), a procedure for selecting model components, e.g., attention heads, to steer a binary concept (e.g., talk in verse vs. talk in prose) from contrastive long-form responses. In GCM, we first construct a dataset of contrasting inputs and responses. Then, we quantify how individual model components mediate the contrastive concept and select the strongest mediators for steering. We evaluate GCM on three tasks--refusal, sycophancy, and style transfer--across three language models. GCM successfully localizes concepts expressed in long-form responses and consistently outperforms correlational probe-based baselines when steering with a sparse set of attention heads. Together, these results demonstrate that GCM provides an effective approach for localizing and controlling the long-form responses of LMs.

papers.title: Towards Best Practices of Activation Patching in Language Models: Metrics and Methods
papers.research_question: How do different methodological choices in activation patching, such as corruption methods and evaluation metrics, affect localization and circuit discovery results in language models?
papers.core_contribution: This paper systematically evaluates hyperparameters in activation patching for language models, finding that choices of corruption methods and metrics significantly affect interpretability results, and provides best practice recommendations.
papers.conclusion: The paper recommends using symmetric token replacement (STR) for in-distribution corruption and logit difference as the evaluation metric for activation patching, highlighting the sensitivity of interpretability results to methodological details.
papers.key_findings:
GN and STR corruption methods lead to inconsistent localization and circuit discovery outcomes.
Probability metric can overlook negative model components that hurt performance, while logit difference is capable of detecting them.
Sliding window patching produces more pronounced localization than summing single-layer patching effects, potentially amplifying weak signals.
GN corruption may put the model off-distribution, breaking internal mechanisms and leading to unreliable interpretability results.
Logit difference is recommended over probability for fine-grained control and detecting negative modules.
papers.abstract: Mechanistic interpretability seeks to understand the internal mechanisms of machine learning models, where localization -- identifying the important model components -- is a key step. Activation patching, also known as causal tracing or interchange intervention, is a standard technique for this task (Vig et al., 2020), but the literature contains many variants with little consensus on the choice of hyperparameters or methodology. In this work, we systematically examine the impact of methodological details in activation patching, including evaluation metrics and corruption methods. In several settings of localization and circuit discovery in language models, we find that varying these hyperparameters could lead to disparate interpretability results. Backed by empirical observations, we give conceptual arguments for why certain metrics or methods may be preferred. Finally, we provide recommendations for the best practices of activation patching going forwards.

papers.title: Compositional generalization in a deep seq2seq model by separating syntax and semantics
papers.research_question: Does separating syntactic and semantic processing in a neural machine translation model improve compositional generalization?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces a novel seq2seq model, Syntactic Attention, which separates syntactic and semantic processing streams. This architectural constraint substantially improves compositional generalization on the SCAN dataset without hand-engineered features or additional supervision.
papers.conclusion: Separating syntactic and semantic information processing in neural networks encourages systematic, compositional generalization, drawing a conceptual link to hypothesized brain mechanisms and suggesting a useful heuristic for AI.
papers.key_findings:
The Syntactic Attention model achieves state-of-the-art performance on the SCAN dataset's add-jump split, with a median accuracy of 91.0%, a significant improvement over prior models.
The model's performance is highly variable across random initializations on the add-jump split, indicating sensitivity to how the novel verb 'jump' is encoded.
Ablation experiments show that allowing sequential information into the semantic stream ('sequential semantics') degrades compositional generalization, supporting the separation hypothesis.
The model generalizes well from very few examples of a novel verb, achieving near-perfect accuracy with just two training examples containing 'jump'.
The model fails on some SCAN template splits (e.g., 'Primitive opposite right'), indicating limitations in generalizing based on symmetry when training data is skewed.
papers.limitation:
The model's performance on the add-jump split is highly variable and skewed across different random initializations, with some runs failing catastrophically.
The separation between syntax and semantics in the brain is likely not as strict as implemented in the model, suggesting the principle may be more of a useful heuristic than a biological fact.
future_direction: Future research should investigate the factors causing performance variability on tasks like the add-jump split and whether other priors or regularization techniques can overcome it.
The principle of separating syntax and semantics may be a useful heuristic in other natural language processing tasks and other systematic or compositional generalization tasks.
papers.abstract: Standard methods in deep learning for natural language processing fail to capture the compositional structure of human language that allows for systematic generalization outside of the training distribution. However, human learners readily generalize in this way, e.g. by applying known grammatical rules to novel words. Inspired by work in neuroscience suggesting separate brain systems for syntactic and semantic processing, we implement a modification to standard approaches in neural machine translation, imposing an analogous separation. The novel model, which we call Syntactic Attention, substantially outperforms standard methods in deep learning on the SCAN dataset, a compositional generalization task, without any hand-engineered features or additional supervision. Our work suggests that separating syntactic from semantic learning may be a useful heuristic for capturing compositional structure.

papers.title: Out-of-distribution generalization via composition: a lens through induction heads in Transformers
papers.research_question: How do Transformers achieve out-of-distribution generalization, specifically through composition and induction heads?
papers.core_contribution: OOD generalization and composition are tied together—models can learn rules by composing two self-attention layers, thereby achieving OOD generalization. A shared latent subspace in the embedding space acts as a bridge for composition, aligning early and later layers (common bridge representation hypothesis).
papers.conclusion: OOD generalization in Transformers is achieved through composition of self-attention layers, with induction heads playing a key role, and the common bridge representation hypothesis offers a plausible explanation for how Transformers generalize compositionally.
papers.key_findings:
OOD generalization is accompanied by abrupt emergence of subspace matching between layers.
Two layers have complementary specialties: position shifting (via previous-token heads) and token matching (via induction heads).
Pattern diversity during training matters for generalization versus memorization.
Induction heads are crucial for symbolized language reasoning tasks in LLMs.
A common bridge subspace aligns many previous-token heads and induction heads in multilayer models, enabling composition.
papers.limitation:
The synthetic example is simple and may not capture the full complexity of natural language.
Intervention experiments on LLMs are correlational and do not establish causality.
The common bridge subspace hypothesis requires further theoretical validation.
future_direction: Analyzing the training dynamics of Transformers for copying and other compositional tasks.
Investigating whether similar mechanisms operate in other architectures, such as state-space models or diffusion models.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) such as GPT-4 sometimes appear to be creative, solving novel tasks often with a few demonstrations in the prompt. These tasks require the models to generalize on distributions different from those from training data -- which is known as out-of-distribution (OOD) generalization. Despite the tremendous success of LLMs, how they approach OOD generalization remains an open and underexplored question. We examine OOD generalization in settings where instances are generated according to hidden rules, including in-context learning with symbolic reasoning. Models are required to infer the hidden rules behind input prompts without any fine-tuning. We empirically examined the training dynamics of Transformers on a synthetic example and conducted extensive experiments on a variety of pretrained LLMs, focusing on a type of components known as induction heads. We found that OOD generalization and composition are tied together -- models can learn rules by composing two self-attention layers, thereby achieving OOD generalization. Furthermore, a shared latent subspace in the embedding (or feature) space acts as a bridge for composition by aligning early layers and later layers, which we refer to as the common bridge representation hypothesis.

papers.title: Compositional Capabilities of Autoregressive Transformers: A Study on Synthetic, Interpretable Tasks
papers.research_question: Can autoregressive Transformers trained on compositional data learn to compose their capabilities and generalize to unseen compositions?
papers.core_contribution: Autoregressive Transformers can learn to compose functions from limited data and generalize to exponentially many unseen compositions, with step-by-step prompting enhancing generalization; attention layers select functions and feed-forward layers execute them.
papers.conclusion: Autoregressive Transformers can learn to compose capabilities from compositional data, with step-by-step prompting and appropriate training data enabling generalization to many unseen compositions; the attention and feed-forward layers play distinct roles in this process.
papers.key_findings:
Autoregressive Transformers can generalize to exponential or combinatorial numbers of unseen function compositions from small training data.
Step-by-step prompting (generating intermediate outputs) significantly improves compositional generalization compared to direct prompting.
Biases in training data (e.g., only in-order compositions) limit out-of-order generalization.
Attention layers are responsible for selecting which function to apply, while feed-forward layers execute the function.
LSTMs fail to compositionally generalize in the same setup, highlighting the importance of Transformer architecture.
papers.limitation: The study is limited to synthetic tasks and may not generalize to real-world language data.
papers.abstract: Transformers trained on huge text corpora exhibit a remarkable set of capabilities, e.g., performing basic arithmetic. Given the inherent compositional nature of language, one can expect the model to learn to compose these capabilities, potentially yielding a combinatorial explosion of what operations it can perform on an input. Motivated by the above, we train autoregressive Transformer models on a synthetic data-generating process that involves compositions of a set of well-defined monolithic capabilities.
