Through a series of extensive and systematic experiments on this data-generating process, we show that: (1) autoregressive Transformers can learn compositional structures from small amounts of training data and generalize to exponentially or even combinatorially many functions; (2) generating intermediate outputs when composing functions is more effective for generalizing to new, unseen compositions than not generating any intermediate outputs (3) biases in the order of the compositions in the training data result in Transformers that fail to compose some combinations of functions; and (4) the attention layers select which capability to apply while the feed-forward layers execute the selected capability.

papers.title: Controllable LLM Reasoning via Sparse Autoencoder-Based Steering
papers.research_question: How can we control fine-grained reasoning strategies in Large Reasoning Models using Sparse Autoencoders to overcome concept entanglement and improve reliability?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces SAE-Steering, a method that uses Sparse Autoencoders to disentangle and identify strategy-specific features for controlling reasoning strategies in Large Reasoning Models, achieving superior control effectiveness and error correction.
papers.conclusion: The work demonstrates that Sparse Autoencoders can disentangle strategy-specific features for fine-grained control of reasoning strategies, with SAE-Steering providing an efficient feature identification pipeline that is effective and robust.
papers.key_findings:
SAE-Steering outperforms existing control methods by over 15% in control effectiveness across various reasoning tasks and models.
The identified SAE features generalize from math to science domains, indicating cross-domain applicability.
Logit-based feature recall is more precise than activation-based methods, improving feature selection accuracy.
Strategy-specific features are prevalent in deeper layers of the model, with optimal control effectiveness in middle-to-late layers.
Controlling reasoning strategies can redirect models from erroneous paths, achieving a 7% absolute accuracy improvement in error correction.
papers.limitation:
Only evaluated five representative reasoning strategies
Only demonstrated application in error correction scenarios
Only attempted to correct erroneous paths by enforcing continued reasoning
future_direction: Investigate controlling other reasoning strategies
Explore applying control to a wider range of applications
Explore guiding the LRM at earlier stages or during intermediate steps
papers.abstract: Large Reasoning Models (LRMs) exhibit human-like cognitive reasoning strategies (e.g. backtracking, cross-verification) during reasoning process, which improves their performance on complex tasks. Currently, reasoning strategies are autonomously selected by LRMs themselves. However, such autonomous selection often produces inefficient or even erroneous reasoning paths. To make reasoning more reliable and flexible, it is important to develop methods for controlling reasoning strategies. Existing methods struggle to control fine-grained reasoning strategies due to conceptual entanglement in LRMs' hidden states. To address this, we leverage Sparse Autoencoders (SAEs) to decompose strategy-entangled hidden states into a disentangled feature space. To identify the few strategy-specific features from the vast pool of SAE features, we propose SAE-Steering, an efficient two-stage feature identification pipeline. SAE-Steering first recalls features that amplify the logits of strategy-specific keywords, filtering out over 99\% of features, and then ranks the remaining features by their control effectiveness. Using the identified strategy-specific features as control vectors, SAE-Steering outperforms existing methods by over 15\% in control effectiveness. Furthermore, controlling reasoning strategies can redirect LRMs from erroneous paths to correct ones, achieving a 7\% absolute accuracy improvement.

papers.title: On Hierarchical Encoding and Reasoning in Deep Transformer-based Generative Models
papers.research_question: How do Transformer models internalize hierarchical structures from data, what is the relationship between this internalization and behaviors like generalization versus memorization, and how can insights into hierarchical reasoning guide the development of more unified, robust, and interpretable multimodal systems?
papers.core_contribution: This thesis investigates how Transformer models learn and represent hierarchical structures, develops methods to probe these structures and mitigate harmful memorization, introduces the PSViT model for hierarchical video prediction, and demonstrates a unified next-frame prediction framework for multimodal tasks.
papers.conclusion: The capacity to learn and represent hierarchical structure is a fundamental characteristic of Transformer models, and a focused analysis of these underpinnings is crucial for advancing more capable, interpretable, and safer artificial intelligence.
papers.key_findings:
Bidirectional Transformer models (e.g., BERT) concentrate hierarchical linguistic information near the top layers, while autoregressive/permutation-masked models (e.g., GPT-2, XLNet, Reformer) distribute it more evenly.
Verbatim memorization during fine-tuning is often preceded by a spike in n-gram overlap, which can be used for early-stopping or regularization to reduce leakage by up to 90%.
The PSViT model, designed with hierarchical priors, outperforms latent-space baselines on physical simulation benchmarks, extending accurate prediction horizons by up to 50%.
Abstract physical parameters governing video dynamics are most linearly recoverable from the middle layers of PSViT, mirroring the mid-layer abstraction peak for linguistic hierarchy.
Diverse tasks across text, image, audio, and video can be reformulated into a unified next-frame prediction task, enabling a single PSViT-based model to achieve competitive performance without modality-specific encoders.
papers.limitation:
Probing tasks relied primarily on English datasets (SST, PTB), limiting linguistic diversity.
Memorization experiments used datasets of up to 5,000 samples and greedy decoding; different scales or decoding strategies may alter dynamics.
PSViT was evaluated at 128x128 resolution on deterministic simulations; generalizability to complex real-world video is untested.
The multimodal model was trained separately per task; joint multitask training might better foster shared representations.
future_direction: Extend ancestor probing to morphologically rich languages, different syntactic formalisms, and broader discourse structures.
Scale the n-gram-aware loss regularizer to operate efficiently on hundreds of billions of tokens.
Test PSViT on larger-scale, stochastic, real-world video and integrate differentiable renderers for more direct interpretability.
Explore joint multitask training on a diverse corpus of reformulated multimodal data and richer encodings within the visual canvas.
papers.abstract: Recent advances in generative Transformer-based foundation models have driven remarkable progress in artificial intelligence, yet their internal mechanisms for representing complex hierarchical structures remain largely unknown, posing significant challenges for interpretability, safety, and robust generalisation. This thesis aims to progress on these issues by systematically investigating how such models internalise hierarchical structures, the relationship between this learning and behaviours like generalisation versus memorisation, and how hierarchical principles can inform the development of safer, more accurate, generative models. To this end, we first introduce novel probing techniques to map the layer-wise emergence of linguistic hierarchies in language models and extend this analysis to the visual domain by developing PSViT: a pixel-space Transformer with hierarchical decompositions of video image patches, shown to learn and generalise hierarchical physical dynamics from raw video data. We investigate memorisation during fine-tuning, establishing an n-gram based early warning signal for verbatim leakage and proposing scalable defences that promote structural generalisation over verbatim memorisation. Building on these insights, we further demonstrate that a unified next-frame prediction framework enables a single model to process text, images, audio, and video without modality-specific encoders, thereby learning shared hierarchical patterns across these diverse inputs. Collectively, our findings underscore that the capacity to learn and represent hierarchical structure is a fundamental characteristic of Transformer models, and that a focused analysis of these underpinnings is crucial for advancing more capable, interpretable, and safer artificial intelligence.

papers.title: Restyling Unsupervised Concept Based Interpretable Networks with Generative Models
papers.research_question: How can we improve the visualization and interpretation of learnt unsupervised concepts in concept-based interpretable networks for large-scale images?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes VisCoIN, a novel architecture for unsupervised concept-based interpretable networks that maps concept features to the latent space of a pretrained generative model, enabling high-quality visualization and interactive interpretation of learnt concepts.
papers.conclusion: VisCoIN effectively leverages pretrained generative models to improve visualization and interpretation of unsupervised concepts in concept-based interpretable networks, achieving high prediction performance and learning more faithful and consistent concepts.
papers.key_findings:
VisCoIN achieves comparable prediction accuracy to baseline methods while improving reconstruction fidelity and perceptual similarity.
The learnt concepts in VisCoIN are more faithful and consistent compared to previous unsupervised CoINs.
The visualization pipeline based on the generative model allows for granular and interactive interpretation of concepts by modifying concept activations and observing changes in generated images.
papers.limitation:
Cannot guarantee that concepts precisely correspond to human concepts and may encode additional information.
System quality is limited by the quality of the pretrained generative model.
Linear trajectories in latent space may not be optimal for latent traversals.
papers.abstract: Developing inherently interpretable models for prediction has gained prominence in recent years. A subclass of these models, wherein the interpretable network relies on learning high-level concepts, are valued because of closeness of concept representations to human communication. However, the visualization and understanding of the learnt unsupervised dictionary of concepts encounters major limitations, especially for large-scale images. We propose here a novel method that relies on mapping the concept features to the latent space of a pretrained generative model. The use of a generative model enables high quality visualization, and lays out an intuitive and interactive procedure for better interpretation of the learnt concepts by imputing concept activations and visualizing generated modifications. Furthermore, leveraging pretrained generative models has the additional advantage of making the training of the system more efficient. We quantitatively ascertain the efficacy of our method in terms of accuracy of the interpretable prediction network, fidelity of reconstruction, as well as faithfulness and consistency of learnt concepts. The experiments are conducted on multiple image recognition benchmarks for large-scale images. Project page available at https://jayneelparekh.github.io/VisCoIN_project_page/

papers.title: Control Reinforcement Learning: Interpretable Token-Level Steering of LLMs via Sparse Autoencoder Features
papers.research_question: How can we identify and amplify sparse autoencoder features that change model outputs at each token to achieve interpretable steering of language models?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces Control Reinforcement Learning (CRL), a framework that trains a policy to select sparse autoencoder features for token-level steering of language models, producing interpretable intervention logs and enabling new analysis capabilities such as branch point tracking and critic trajectory analysis.
papers.conclusion: Learned feature steering with CRL establishes a mechanistic interpretability tool that complements static feature analysis with dynamic intervention probes.
papers.key_findings:
CRL improves performance on MMLU, BBQ, GSM8K, HarmBench, and XSTest while providing interpretable per-token intervention logs.
Branch point tracking locates tokens where feature selection determines output correctness.
Critic trajectory analysis distinguishes between policy limitations and critic estimation errors.
Layer-wise analysis shows that early layers encode syntactic patterns while later layers capture abstract semantics.
Adaptive Feature Masking (AFM) prevents policy collapse and encourages diverse feature discovery.
papers.limitation:
The method introduces 8-9% inference latency overhead.
The method does not generalize equally to all tasks and models, as seen by performance decline on XSTest for LLaMA-3.1 8B.
papers.abstract: Sparse autoencoders (SAEs) decompose language model activations into interpretable features, but existing methods reveal only which features activate, not which change model outputs when amplified. We introduce Control Reinforcement Learning (CRL), which trains a policy to select SAE features for steering at each token, producing interpretable intervention logs: the learned policy identifies features that change model outputs when amplified. Adaptive Feature Masking encourages diverse feature discovery while preserving singlefeature interpretability. The framework yields new analysis capabilities: branch point tracking locates tokens where feature choice determines output correctness; critic trajectory analysis separates policy limitations from value estimation errors; layer-wise comparison reveals syntactic features in early layers and semantic features in later layers. On Gemma 2 2B across MMLU, BBQ, GSM8K, HarmBench, and XSTest, CRL achieves improvements while providing per-token intervention logs. These results establish learned feature steering as a mechanistic interpretability tool that complements static feature analysis with dynamic intervention probes

papers.title: Analyzing Vision Transformers for Image Classification in Class Embedding Space
papers.research_question: How do Vision Transformers build categorical representations for image classification, and how do self-attention and MLP layers contribute to this process?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces a framework to project Vision Transformers' internal representations onto the class embedding space, enabling analysis of how class representations are built and the differential roles of self-attention and MLP layers via key-value memory pair mechanisms.
papers.conclusion: The proposed framework is a powerful tool for mechanistic interpretability and explainability of Vision Transformers, providing insights into their category-building processes.
papers.key_findings:
Image tokens develop class-specific representations from early stages, with class identifiability increasing across blocks.
Attention mechanisms and contextual information are crucial for building class representations; image tokens cannot develop class-identifiable representations in isolation.
Self-attention and MLP layers differentially contribute: MLP layers promote strong categorical updates in late blocks, while self-attention layers promote weaker but more disseminated updates earlier.
The framework can identify image regions important for class detection and outperforms linear probing in revealing task-relevant features.
Key-value memory pair mechanisms in MLP and self-attention layers are involved in building class representations, with agreement rates correlating with model accuracy.
papers.limitation:
Only studies Vision Transformers trained for image classification.
Does not explore model editing or performance improvement applications.
future_direction: Adapt the framework to models with other types of output embeddings.
Use the mechanistic insights for model editing or performance improvement.
papers.abstract: Despite the growing use of transformer models in computer vision, a mechanistic understanding of these networks is still needed. This work introduces a method to reverse-engineer Vision Transformers trained to solve image classification tasks. Inspired by previous research in NLP, we demonstrate how the inner representations at any level of the hierarchy can be projected onto the learned class embedding space to uncover how these networks build categorical representations for their predictions. We use our framework to show how image tokens develop class-specific representations that depend on attention mechanisms and contextual information, and give insights on how self-attention and MLP layers differentially contribute to this categorical composition. We additionally demonstrate that this method (1) can be used to determine the parts of an image that would be important for detecting the class of interest, and (2) exhibits significant advantages over traditional linear probing approaches. Taken together, our results position our proposed framework as a powerful tool for mechanistic interpretability and explainability research.

papers.title: Beyond Interpretability: The Gains of Feature Monosemanticity on Model Robustness
papers.research_question: Does feature monosemanticity, which improves interpretability, also improve model robustness, challenging the accuracy-interpretability tradeoff?
papers.core_contribution: This paper challenges the accuracy-interpretability tradeoff by showing that monosemantic features not only enhance interpretability but also provide concrete gains in model robustness across various scenarios including noise, few-shot learning, and out-of-domain generalization.
papers.conclusion: The study demonstrates that monosemanticity offers advantages beyond interpretability, improving model robustness across multiple learning scenarios, and advocates for exploring its broader learning benefits.
papers.key_findings:
Monosemantic features (from NCL or SAE) are more robust than polysemantic features under linear probing with label noise and input noise.
Maintaining monosemanticity during finetuning (via non-negative tuning) reduces overfitting and improves performance in few-shot and noisy-label settings.
MonoLoRA, a sparse variant of LoRA, better preserves alignment safety while maintaining task performance when finetuning LLMs on small datasets.
Empirical analysis shows that classifiers with higher robustness under noise rely more on monosemantic features.
Theoretical analysis on a toy model indicates monosemantic features have better linear separability under noise, leading to more robust decision boundaries.
papers.abstract: Deep learning models often suffer from a lack of interpretability due to polysemanticity, where individual neurons are activated by multiple unrelated semantics, resulting in unclear attributions of model behavior. Recent advances in monosemanticity, where neurons correspond to consistent and distinct semantics, have significantly improved interpretability but are commonly believed to compromise accuracy. In this work, we challenge the prevailing belief of the accuracy-interpretability tradeoff, showing that monosemantic features not only enhance interpretability but also bring concrete gains in model performance. Across multiple robust learning scenarios-including input and label noise, few-shot learning, and out-of-domain generalization-our results show that models leveraging monosemantic features significantly outperform those relying on polysemantic features. Furthermore, we provide empirical and theoretical understandings on the robustness gains of feature monosemanticity. Our preliminary analysis suggests that monosemanticity, by promoting better separation of feature representations, leads to more robust decision boundaries. This diverse evidence highlights the generality of monosemanticity in improving model robustness. As a first step in this new direction, we embark on exploring the learning benefits of monosemanticity beyond interpretability, supporting the long-standing hypothesis of linking interpretability and robustness. Code is available at \url{https://github.com/PKU-ML/Beyond_Interpretability}.

papers.title: Compositional generalization through abstract representations in human and artificial neural networks
papers.research_question: What are the computational properties of compositional generalization in humans and artificial neural networks, and how can pretraining induce abstract representations that support such generalization?
papers.core_contribution: Pretraining ANNs with primitives induces abstract representations that support compositional generalization, matching human behavior and neural data.
papers.conclusion: Pretraining with primitives embeds abstract representations into ANNs, enabling compositional generalization that recapitulates human behavior and neural representations.
papers.key_findings:
Humans show compositional generalization in behavior, with performance improving with rule overlap and practice.
Abstract representations (high Parallelism Score) are found in human cortex, with content-specific topography.
Pretraining ANNs with primitives induces abstract representations, leading to high zero-shot generalization and sample efficiency.
The hierarchy of abstract representations in pretrained ANNs matches the sensory-to-motor hierarchy in human cortex.
Pretraining facilitates human-like compositional generalization in ANNs, with performance similar to humans on novel contexts.
future_direction: Explore the ordering of pretraining paradigms for generalization performance and sample efficiency.
papers.abstract: Humans have a remarkable ability to rapidly generalize to new tasks that is difficult to reproduce in artificial learning systems. Compositionality has been proposed as a key mechanism supporting generalization in humans, but evidence of its neural implementation and impact on behavior is still scarce. Here we study the computational properties associated with compositional generalization in both humans and artificial neural networks (ANNs) on a highly compositional task. First, we identified behavioral signatures of compositional generalization in humans, along with their neural correlates using whole-cortex functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) data. Next, we designed pretraining paradigms aided by a procedure we term {\em primitives pretraining} to endow compositional task elements into ANNs. We found that ANNs with this prior knowledge had greater correspondence with human behavior and neural compositional signatures. Importantly, primitives pretraining induced abstract internal representations, excellent zero-shot generalization, and sample-efficient learning. Moreover, it gave rise to a hierarchy of abstract representations that matched human fMRI data, where sensory rule abstractions emerged in early sensory areas, and motor rule abstractions emerged in later motor areas. Our findings give empirical support to the role of compositional generalization in human behavior, implicate abstract representations as its neural implementation, and illustrate that these representations can be embedded into ANNs by designing simple and efficient pretraining procedures.

papers.title: Designing Role Vectors to Improve LLM Inference Behaviour
papers.research_question: Can we identify specific latent role directions within the activation space that lead to improved performance on objective tasks? Do these directions effectively impersonate the role of interest? Does eliminating these directions degrade performance?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces role vectors as a method to steer LLM behavior by manipulating internal activations, showing that this can improve performance in domain-specific tasks.
papers.conclusion: Role vectors offer a promising pathway for achieving more controllable behaviour in large language models.
papers.key_findings:
Role vectors can steer models to improve performance in target domains.
Larger models show more interpretable role directions.
Only a subset of directions align with intended roles.
Ablating role directions can degrade performance in target domains.
Steering effects are sensitive to model scale and intervention depth.
papers.limitation:
Results might differ in untested models, especially larger ones.
Lack of a complete mechanistic explanation of the phenomenon.
Uncertain semantic interpretation of the identified directions.
Potential degradation in performance in unrelated tasks.
Possible reinforcement of biases or over-confidence.
future_direction: Using Activation Patching (Causal Mediation Analysis) techniques with SAE features to better explain the phenomenon.
Exploring additional analytical dimensions and potential biases.
papers.abstract: The influence of personas on Large Language Models (LLMs) has been widely studied, yet their direct impact on performance remains uncertain. This work explores a novel approach to guiding LLM behaviour through role vectors, an alternative to persona-based prompting. We construct 29 role vectors derived from model activations and evaluate their impact on benchmark performance across multiple domains. Our analysis investigates whether these vectors can effectively steer models toward domain-specific expertise. We measure two key interventions: (i) activation addition, which reinforces role-specific directions, and (ii) directional ablation, which removes them. Results on well-established benchmarks indicate that role vectors do, in fact, influence model behaviour, improving task performance in relevant domains while marginally affecting unrelated tasks. This, in turn, suggests that manipulating internal model representations has a greater impact on outcomes than persona-based prompting.

papers.title: Towards Faithful Natural Language Explanations: A Study Using Activation Patching in Large Language Models
papers.research_question: How can we measure the faithfulness of natural language explanations generated by LLMs using causal mediation techniques like activation patching, and how do different models and alignment-tuning affect explanation faithfulness?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces Causal Faithfulness (CaF), a metric that uses activation patching to measure the faithfulness of natural language explanations by comparing the causal attributions of the answer and explanation, addressing limitations of prior methods.
papers.conclusion: The paper introduces Causal Faithfulness, a metric using activation patching to assess explanation faithfulness by comparing causal distributions, and highlights the importance of avoiding out-of-distribution inputs in faithfulness evaluation.
papers.key_findings:
Instruct-tuned models produce more faithful explanations than pre-trained models.
There is a positive correlation between explanation plausibility and faithfulness.
Activation patching avoids out-of-distribution issues that affect SHAP-based methods.
Causal Faithfulness is a more theoretically sound faithfulness metric compared to existing surface-level tests.
Models attribute higher causal importance to corrupted tokens and consider alternative answer choices during reasoning.
papers.limitation:
Increased computational requirements due to T·L forward passes
Token replacement requires the set of edited tokens to be of equal length to the tokens being replaced
Activation patching primarily provides insights starting from the corrupted spans onward, limiting the scope of information revealed
future_direction: Integrating mechanistic interpretability approaches for a more robust faithfulness assessment framework.
Exploring methods for variable-length token replacement to relax the equal-length constraint.

papers.title: Causal Mediation Analysis for Interpreting Neural NLP: The Case of Gender Bias
papers.research_question: How can causal mediation analysis be used to interpret the internal mechanisms of neural NLP models, specifically to understand the role of individual components (like neurons and attention heads) in mediating gender bias?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces a structural-behavioral framework based on causal mediation analysis for interpreting neural NLP models, and applies it to gender bias, revealing that bias effects are sparse, synergistic, and decomposable into direct and indirect effects.
papers.conclusion: Causal mediation analysis provides a useful framework for interpreting neural NLP models, offering insights into the internal mechanisms by which properties like gender bias flow from input to output through various model components.
papers.key_findings:
Gender bias effects are sparse, concentrated in a relatively small number of model components (neurons and attention heads).
Gender bias effects are synergistic, with different model components interacting to amplify or repress their individual effects.
Gender bias effects are decomposable, with the total effect approximating the sum of direct and indirect effects, despite model non-linearity.
Larger models tend to exhibit larger gender bias effects.
The causal mediation analysis framework captures general patterns of causal structure in Transformer architectures, not just model-specific characteristics.
papers.limitation:
The experimental design focuses on gender bias in a binary setup, which does not account for a gender-inclusive spectrum.
Preliminary experiments with gender-neutral references (e.g., singular 'they') showed models have not learned these concepts well, and the setup suffers from confounders like plural 'they'.
Results for masked language models (e.g., BERT) are less clear, potentially due to differences in scoring multi-token continuations compared to autoregressive models.
future_direction: Applying the methodology to more gender-inclusive setups and other kinds of biases.
Using mediation analysis to guide the development of new debiasing methods that establish counterfactual fairness.
Exploring path-specific effects to identify exact mechanisms through which biases arise.
papers.abstract: Common methods for interpreting neural models in natural language processing typically examine either their structure or their behavior, but not both. We propose a methodology grounded in the theory of causal mediation analysis for interpreting which parts of a model are causally implicated in its behavior. It enables us to analyze the mechanisms by which information flows from input to output through various model components, known as mediators. We apply this methodology to analyze gender bias in pre-trained Transformer language models. We study the role of individual neurons and attention heads in mediating gender bias across three datasets designed to gauge a model's sensitivity to gender bias. Our mediation analysis reveals that gender bias effects are (i) sparse, concentrated in a small part of the network; (ii) synergistic, amplified or repressed by different components; and (iii) decomposable into effects flowing directly from the input and indirectly through the mediators.

papers.title: AtMan: Understanding Transformer Predictions Through Memory Efficient Attention Manipulation
papers.research_question: How can we provide explanations for generative transformer models in a memory-efficient way, avoiding the high memory cost of gradient-based methods?
papers.core_contribution: ATMAN is a memory-efficient, perturbation-based explainability method for generative transformers that manipulates attention scores and uses correlated token suppression via cosine similarity in the embedding space, providing explanations without backpropagation.
papers.conclusion: ATMAN is an effective, memory-efficient explainability method for generative transformer models that outperforms gradient-based approaches and scales to large models, enabling explanation capabilities in production deployments.
papers.key_findings:
ATMAN outperforms gradient-based XAI methods (e.g., Chefer et al., IG, IxG) on text (SQuAD) and image-text (OpenImages) benchmarks in terms of mean average precision and recall.
ATMAN requires almost no extra memory compared to a forward pass, making it scalable to large models (e.g., 30B parameters) where gradient-based methods fail due to memory constraints.
The method is modality-agnostic and works on both decoder (e.g., GPT-J, MAGMA) and encoder-decoder (e.g., BLIP) transformer architectures.
Correlated token suppression using cosine similarity in the embedding space improves explanation quality by suppressing redundant information across tokens, especially in vision tasks.
ATMAN can be run in parallel, and its runtime can be reduced to near forward-pass levels with batching and pipeline parallelism.
papers.limitation:
The question of 'what an explanation is' remains undefined, and the method may highlight input features that lead to diverging generations even if they do not match human expectations.
There are many promising variants of ATMAN (e.g., layer-specific manipulations, different similarity measures) that are not yet fully understood and require future research.
future_direction: Study whether models' explanatory capabilities scale with their size.
Investigate variants of ATMAN, such as using different similarity measures (e.g., BERT embeddings for NLP), layer-specific manipulations, or hierarchical token aggregation for speed.
Explore the use of ATMAN for instructing and improving model predictions based on human feedback on explanations.
papers.abstract: Generative transformer models have become increasingly complex, with large numbers of parameters and the ability to process multiple input modalities. Current methods for explaining their predictions are resource-intensive. Most crucially, they require prohibitively large amounts of extra memory, since they rely on backpropagation which allocates almost twice as much GPU memory as the forward pass. This makes it difficult, if not impossible, to use them in production. We present AtMan that provides explanations of generative transformer models at almost no extra cost. Specifically, AtMan is a modality-agnostic perturbation method that manipulates the attention mechanisms of transformers to produce relevance maps for the input with respect to the output prediction. Instead of using backpropagation, AtMan applies a parallelizable token-based search method based on cosine similarity neighborhood in the embedding space. Our exhaustive experiments on text and image-text benchmarks demonstrate that AtMan outperforms current state-of-the-art gradient-based methods on several metrics while being computationally efficient. As such, AtMan is suitable for use in large model inference deployments.

papers.title: Residual Connections Harm Generative Representation Learning
papers.research_question: Do residual connections harm generative representation learning, and can modifying them by decaying the identity shortcuts improve feature learning?
papers.core_contribution: Introducing decayed identity shortcuts, a simple architectural modification that downweights residual connections with depth, significantly improves semantic feature learning in generative representation learning frameworks like MAEs and diffusion models without adding learnable parameters.
papers.conclusion: Residual connections may be suboptimal for representation learning; the proposed decayed identity shortcuts improve unsupervised representation learning and are correlated with low-rank features, prompting further investigation into architectural reparameterizations.
papers.key_findings:
Decayed identity shortcuts raise ImageNet-1K linear probing accuracy from 67.8% to 72.7% and KNN accuracy from 27.4% to 63.9% for MAE with ViT-B/16.
The method improves generation quality in diffusion models, lowering FID scores.
Improvements are correlated with lower effective feature rank, indicating a low-rank inductive bias.
Smaller models with decayed identity shortcuts can outperform larger models with standard residual connections.
The method does not compromise reconstruction quality in MAEs.
papers.limitation: The method does not easily extend to contrastive learning frameworks because the low-rank inductive bias conflicts with their training objectives.
future_direction: Further reparametrizations and improvements to unsupervised representation learning.
More extensive investigations into the connection between low effective rank and high-quality abstract representations.
Exploration of underlying theoretical mechanisms for the relationship between low rank and good representations.
papers.abstract: We show that introducing a weighting factor to reduce the influence of identity shortcuts in residual networks significantly enhances semantic feature learning in generative representation learning frameworks, such as masked autoencoders (MAEs) and diffusion models. Our modification notably improves feature quality, raising ImageNet-1K K-Nearest Neighbor accuracy from 27.4% to 63.9% and linear probing accuracy from 67.8% to 72.7% for MAEs with a ViT-B/16 backbone, while also enhancing generation quality in diffusion models. This significant gap suggests that, while residual connection structure serves an essential role in facilitating gradient propagation, it may have a harmful side effect of reducing capacity for abstract learning by virtue of injecting an echo of shallower representations into deeper layers. We ameliorate this downside via a fixed formula for monotonically decreasing the contribution of identity connections as layer depth increases. Our design promotes the gradual development of feature abstractions, without impacting network trainability. Analyzing the representations learned by our modified residual networks, we find correlation between low effective feature rank and downstream task performance.

papers.title: A Unified Theory of Sparse Dictionary Learning in Mechanistic Interpretability: Piecewise Biconvexity and Spurious Minima
papers.research_question: Why do sparse dictionary learning (SDL) methods consistently produce polysemantic features, feature absorption, and dead neurons, and what is the theoretical understanding of these phenomena?
papers.core_contribution: Develops a unified theoretical framework for sparse dictionary learning (SDL) that explains failure modes like feature absorption and dead neurons via piecewise biconvex optimization and non-identifiability, and proposes feature anchoring to improve feature recovery.
papers.conclusion: The theoretical framework explains persistent failure modes in SDL methods, and feature anchoring provides an effective, method-agnostic technique to improve feature recovery by reducing underdetermination.
papers.key_findings:
SDL optimization exhibits piecewise biconvex structure, enabling analysis of its landscape.
SDL suffers from non-identifiability, leading to spurious minima that result in polysemantic features.
Feature absorption arises naturally from hierarchical concept structures and corresponds to partial minima.
Feature anchoring, which constrains a subset of features to known directions, significantly improves feature recovery across SDL methods.
Dead neuron resampling helps escape spurious local minima in large language models.
papers.limitation:
Theoretical analysis relies on the Linear Representation Hypothesis, which assumes features are linear directions; this may not hold for all representations.
The synthetic benchmark, while controlled, may not capture all complexities of real-world data.
Feature anchoring requires anchor features, which may be difficult to obtain in some settings.
future_direction: Extending the theory to non-linear representations.
Applying feature anchoring to more domains and real-world tasks.
Integrating anchoring with other SDL improvements and scaling to larger models.
papers.abstract: As AI models achieve remarkable capabilities across diverse domains, understanding what representations they learn and how they encode concepts has become increasingly important for both scientific progress and trustworthy deployment. Recent works in mechanistic interpretability have widely reported that neural networks represent meaningful concepts as linear directions in their representation spaces and often encode diverse concepts in superposition. Various sparse dictionary learning (SDL) methods, including sparse autoencoders, transcoders, and crosscoders, are utilized to address this by training auxiliary models with sparsity constraints to disentangle these superposed concepts into monosemantic features. These methods are the backbone of modern mechanistic interpretability, yet in practice they consistently produce polysemantic features, feature absorption, and dead neurons, with very limited theoretical understanding of why these phenomena occur. Existing theoretical work is limited to tied-weight sparse autoencoders, leaving the broader family of SDL methods without formal grounding. We develop the first unified theoretical framework that casts all major SDL variants as a single piecewise biconvex optimization problem, and characterize its global solution set, non-identifiability, and spurious optima. This analysis yields principled explanations for feature absorption and dead neurons. To expose these pathologies under full ground-truth access, we introduce the Linear Representation Bench. Guided by our theory, we propose feature anchoring, a novel technique that restores SDL identifiability, substantially improving feature recovery across synthetic benchmarks and real neural representations.

papers.title: AxBench: Steering LLMs? Even Simple Baselines Outperform Sparse Autoencoders
papers.research_question: How do various representation-based steering methods compare to prompting and finetuning in terms of concept detection and model steering for language models?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces AXBENCH, a benchmark for evaluating steering and concept detection methods, and finds that prompting outperforms representation-based methods for steering, while difference-in-means and probes are best for detection, with the novel ReFT-r1 method being competitive on both tasks.
papers.conclusion: Representation steering methods largely lag behind prompting and finetuning, but ReFT-r1 shows that steering can be improved with comprehensive benchmarks.
papers.key_findings:
Prompting is the best method for model steering, outperforming all representation-based methods.
Difference-in-means, linear probes, and ReFT-r1 perform best for concept detection with no significant difference between them.
Sparse autoencoders (SAEs) are not competitive compared to other methods on both steering and detection.
ReFT-r1, a novel weakly-supervised method, is competitive on both steering and detection tasks while offering interpretability advantages.
The AXBENCH benchmark enables comprehensive evaluation and comparison of steering methods.
papers.limitation: Hyperparameter tuning might underestimate steering performance due to limited compute resources.
future_direction: Extend AXBENCH to arbitrary concept descriptions and add new evaluation tasks as better feature-labelling techniques and steering approaches emerge.
papers.abstract: Fine-grained steering of language model outputs is essential for safety and reliability. Prompting and finetuning are widely used to achieve these goals, but interpretability researchers have proposed a variety of representation-based techniques as well, including sparse autoencoders (SAEs), linear artificial tomography, supervised steering vectors, linear probes, and representation finetuning. At present, there is no benchmark for making direct comparisons between these proposals. Therefore, we introduce AxBench, a large-scale benchmark for steering and concept detection, and report experiments on Gemma-2-2B and 9B. For steering, we find that prompting outperforms all existing methods, followed by finetuning. For concept detection, representation-based methods such as difference-in-means, perform the best. On both evaluations, SAEs are not competitive. We introduce a novel weakly-supervised representational method (Rank-1 Representation Finetuning; ReFT-r1), which is competitive on both tasks while providing the interpretability advantages that prompting lacks. Along with AxBench, we train and publicly release SAE-scale feature dictionaries for ReFT-r1 and DiffMean.

papers.title: Exploring Compositionality in Vision Transformers using Wavelet Representations
papers.research_question: Does the Vision Transformer (ViT) encoder exhibit compositionality in its representations? Specifically, can the representation of an image be composed from the representations of its wavelet primitives?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces a framework to test compositionality in ViT encoder representations using Discrete Wavelet Transform (DWT) primitives and shows that ViT encoder representations are approximately compositional for one-level DWT decomposition.
papers.conclusion: ViT encoder representations exhibit compositional behavior when using primitives from a one-level DWT decomposition, providing a new perspective on how ViTs structure information.
papers.key_findings:
Simple summation of wavelet primitive representations does not reconstruct the original image's representation, indicating a lack of strict compositionality under addition.
A learnable linear composition function can approximate the original image's representation from the wavelet primitive representations, especially for one-level DWT decomposition.
The learned composition function assigns significantly higher weight to the low-pass (approximation) sub-band compared to detail sub-bands.
The proposed compositionality framework is robust to image distortions such as JPEG compression and additive Gaussian noise.
Compositionality is observed in the final encoder layer of ViT models (ViT-B and ViT-L) when using one-level DWT decomposition.
papers.limitation: The analysis is restricted to the final encoder layer of the ViT.
future_direction: Explore all encoder layers of the ViT for potential compositionality.
Explore other ways to study the error in composition.
papers.abstract: While insights into the workings of the transformer model have largely emerged by analysing their behaviour on language tasks, this work investigates the representations learnt by the Vision Transformer (ViT) encoder through the lens of compositionality. We introduce a framework, analogous to prior work on measuring compositionality in representation learning, to test for compositionality in the ViT encoder. Crucial to drawing this analogy is the Discrete Wavelet Transform (DWT), which is a simple yet effective tool for obtaining input-dependent primitives in the vision setting. By examining the ability of composed representations to reproduce original image representations, we empirically test the extent to which compositionality is respected in the representation space. Our findings show that primitives from a one-level DWT decomposition produce encoder representations that approximately compose in latent space, offering a new perspective on how ViTs structure information.

papers.title: Measuring and Guiding Monosemanticity
papers.research_question: How can we systematically measure and improve the monosemanticity (single-concept encoding) of feature representations in large language models, specifically within Sparse Autoencoders?
papers.core_contribution: This paper introduces the Feature Monosemanticity Score (FMS), a novel metric for quantifying monosemanticity in latent representations, and proposes Guided Sparse Autoencoders (G-SAE), a method that uses latent conditioning during training to enforce isolated, monosemantic feature representations, improving interpretability and control.
papers.conclusion: The introduced FMS metric and G-SAE method provide actionable guidelines for advancing mechanistic interpretability and control of LLMs by enabling reliable measurement and enforcement of monosemantic feature representations.
papers.key_findings:
G-SAE achieves significantly higher FMS scores than vanilla SAEs, indicating stronger feature monosemanticity, localization, and disentanglement.
G-SAE enables more effective and precise concept detection (e.g., toxicity, writing style, privacy attributes) compared to unsupervised SAEs.
Steering using G-SAE's decoder vectors allows for fine-grained control over model outputs (e.g., reducing toxicity, altering writing style) with less quality degradation than baseline methods.
The proposed FMS metric reveals critical shortcomings in the monosemanticity of features learned by standard, unsupervised SAEs.
papers.limitation:
The training of G-SAE requires labeled data for the target concepts, which may not always be available.
The method could be misused for adversarial steering to amplify undesirable model behaviors.
papers.abstract: There is growing interest in leveraging mechanistic interpretability and controllability to better understand and influence the internal dynamics of large language models (LLMs). However, current methods face fundamental challenges in reliably localizing and manipulating feature representations. Sparse Autoencoders (SAEs) have recently emerged as a promising direction for feature extraction at scale, yet they, too, are limited by incomplete feature isolation and unreliable monosemanticity. To systematically quantify these limitations, we introduce Feature Monosemanticity Score (FMS), a novel metric to quantify feature monosemanticity in latent representation. Building on these insights, we propose Guided Sparse Autoencoders (G-SAE), a method that conditions latent representations on labeled concepts during training. We demonstrate that reliable localization and disentanglement of target concepts within the latent space improve interpretability, detection of behavior, and control. Specifically, our evaluations on toxicity detection, writing style identification, and privacy attribute recognition show that G-SAE not only enhances monosemanticity but also enables more effective and fine-grained steering with less quality degradation. Our findings provide actionable guidelines for measuring and advancing mechanistic interpretability and control of LLMs.

papers.title: From Flat to Hierarchical: Extracting Sparse Representations with Matching Pursuit
papers.research_question: The paper investigates whether sparse autoencoders (SAEs) can capture hierarchical and nonlinearly accessible features in neural network representations, and whether a new SAE architecture (MP-SAE) can better capture such structures.
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces MP-SAE, a sparse autoencoder based on matching pursuit, which captures hierarchical and nonlinearly accessible features in neural representations, outperforming existing SAEs and revealing cross-modal structure in vision-language models.
papers.conclusion: The paper concludes that interpretability methods should be grounded in the phenomenology of representations, and that MP-SAE provides a step in this direction by capturing hierarchical and nonlinear structures.
papers.key_findings:
Existing SAEs struggle to capture conditionally orthogonal (hierarchical) features, while MP-SAE can capture both intra-level and inter-level structure.
MP-SAE recovers more expressive features than standard SAEs across various vision models, achieving higher reconstruction accuracy at comparable sparsity.
MP-SAE enables adaptive sparsity at inference time, allowing monotonic improvement in reconstruction error with each step, unlike fixed-sparsity SAEs.
MP-SAE learns dictionaries with higher global coherence but selects less interfering features at inference, promoting conditional orthogonality.
MP-SAE uncovers multimodal features in vision-language models that are shared across modalities, whereas standard SAEs tend to learn modality-specific features.
papers.limitation:
The analysis is limited to hierarchical and nonlinear structures; other forms of structure (e.g., multi-dimensional features) are not addressed.
MP-SAE's inference requires multiple steps, which may be computationally more expensive than standard SAEs.
future_direction: Extending MP-SAE to capture multi-dimensional features.
Applying MP-SAE to larger-scale language models and more complex tasks.
papers.abstract: Motivated by the hypothesis that neural network representations encode abstract, interpretable features as linearly accessible, approximately orthogonal directions, sparse autoencoders (SAEs) have become a popular tool in interpretability. However, recent work has demonstrated phenomenology of model representations that lies outside the scope of this hypothesis, showing signatures of hierarchical, nonlinear, and multi-dimensional features. This raises the question: do SAEs represent features that possess structure at odds with their motivating hypothesis? If not, does avoiding this mismatch help identify said features and gain further insights into neural network representations? To answer these questions, we take a construction-based approach and re-contextualize the popular matching pursuits (MP) algorithm from sparse coding to design MP-SAE -- an SAE that unrolls its encoder into a sequence of residual-guided steps, allowing it to capture hierarchical and nonlinearly accessible features. Comparing this architecture with existing SAEs on a mixture of synthetic and natural data settings, we show: (i) hierarchical concepts induce conditionally orthogonal features, which existing SAEs are unable to faithfully capture, and (ii) the nonlinear encoding step of MP-SAE recovers highly meaningful features, helping us unravel shared structure in the seemingly dichotomous representation spaces of different modalities in a vision-language model, hence demonstrating the assumption that useful features are solely linearly accessible is insufficient. We also show that the sequential encoder principle of MP-SAE affords an additional benefit of adaptive sparsity at inference time, which may be of independent interest. Overall, we argue our results provide credence to the idea that interpretability should begin with the phenomenology of representations, with methods emerging from assumptions that fit it.

papers.title: Transformers Use Causal World Models in Maze-Solving Tasks
papers.research_question: Do transformers trained on maze-solving tasks acquire causal world models, and how are these models structured and used?
papers.core_contribution: Transformers trained on maze-solving tasks develop causal world models, with interventions revealing an asymmetry (activation easier than suppression) and positional encodings affect the world model structure.
papers.conclusion: Transformers trained on maze-solving tasks form causal world models that capture maze connectivity, and these representations are used for solving.
papers.key_findings:
Transformers trained on maze-solving tasks acquire causally relevant world models.
Interventions that activate features are more effective than those that remove them (asymmetry).
Models can reason about mazes with more simultaneously active features than seen during training, but fail when the same mazes are provided via longer input sequences.
Positional encoding schemes influence how world models are structured (e.g., Stan uses a compositional code, Terry uses single features).
SAEs are better than linear probes for isolating world models.
papers.limitation: Stan was unable to generalize to sequences containing more connections than it had seen during training, leading to failure in removal interventions.
future_direction: Future research could explore how to impose constraints on AI systems in terms of the features they acquire as a result of training.
Future work could investigate how these findings generalize to more complex environments and tasks.
papers.abstract: Recent studies in interpretability have explored the inner workings of transformer models trained on tasks across various domains, often discovering that these networks naturally develop highly structured representations. When such representations comprehensively reflect the task domain's structure, they are commonly referred to as "World Models" (WMs). In this work, we identify WMs in transformers trained on maze-solving tasks. By using Sparse Autoencoders (SAEs) and analyzing attention patterns, we examine the construction of WMs and demonstrate consistency between SAE feature-based and circuit-based analyses. By subsequently intervening on isolated features to confirm their causal role, we find that it is easier to activate features than to suppress them. Furthermore, we find that models can reason about mazes involving more simultaneously active features than they encountered during training; however, when these same mazes (with greater numbers of connections) are provided to models via input tokens instead, the models fail. Finally, we demonstrate that positional encoding schemes appear to influence how World Models are structured within the model's residual stream.

papers.title: Mechanistic understanding and validation of large AI models with SemanticLens
papers.research_question: How can we achieve automated explanation and validation of model components at scale to understand their inner knowledge and ensure alignment with human expectations?
papers.core_contribution: SemanticLens is a universal explanation method that embeds neural network components into the semantic space of a foundation model, enabling scalable search, description, comparison, and auditing of learned concepts for component-level understanding and validation.
papers.conclusion: By enabling component-level understanding and validation, SemanticLens helps mitigate the opacity of AI models, facilitating more reliable deployment in critical applications.
papers.key_findings:
SemanticLens enables text-based search to identify neurons encoding specific concepts, such as biases or data artefacts, in models like ResNet50v2.
It can describe and structure the internal knowledge of models through semantic embeddings, revealing clusters of concepts like animals and vehicles.
The method allows auditing of concept alignment with expected reasoning, detecting spurious correlations and measuring reliance on valid vs. spurious concepts.
In medical image analysis, SemanticLens identifies spurious components (e.g., scale bars, band-aids) and enables model correction via pruning or retraining, improving robustness.
It introduces interpretability measures (clarity, polysemanticity, redundancy) that correlate with human perception and vary across architectures and training regimes.
papers.limitation: Concepts may be distributed across several components, and the neural basis may not comprehensively capture all relevant concepts.
papers.abstract: Abstract Unlike human-engineered systems, such as aeroplanes, for which the role and dependencies of each component are well understood, the inner workings of artificial intelligence models remain largely opaque, which hinders verifiability and undermines trust. Current approaches to neural network interpretability, including input attribution methods, probe-based analysis and activation visualization techniques, typically provide limited insights about the role of individual components or require extensive manual interpretation that cannot scale with model complexity. This paper introduces SemanticLens, a universal explanation method for neural networks that maps hidden knowledge encoded by components (for example, individual neurons) into the semantically structured, multimodal space of a foundation model such as CLIP. In this space, unique operations become possible, including (1) textual searches to identify neurons encoding specific concepts, (2) systematic analysis and comparison of model representations, (3) automated labelling of neurons and explanation of their functional roles, and (4) audits to validate decision-making against requirements. Fully scalable and operating without human input, SemanticLens is shown to be effective for debugging and validation, summarizing model knowledge, aligning reasoning with expectations (for example, adherence to the ABCDE rule in melanoma classification) and detecting components tied to spurious correlations and their associated training data. By enabling component-level understanding and validation, the proposed approach helps mitigate the opacity that limits confidence in artificial intelligence systems compared to traditional engineered systems, enabling more reliable deployment in critical applications.

papers.title: Interpretable LLM Guardrails via Sparse Representation Steering
papers.research_question: How can we achieve fine-grained and interpretable control over LLM behavior to mitigate harmful, misleading, or biased content using sparse representation steering?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces SRS, a framework that uses sparse autoencoders to disentangle activations into monosemantic features and steer LLM behavior via sparse steering vectors, achieving fine-grained control while preserving output quality.
papers.conclusion: SRS enables precise and interpretable steering of LLM behavior using sparse representations, providing a reliable guardrail for safety, fairness, and truthfulness with superior performance over existing methods.
papers.key_findings:
SRS outperforms existing steering methods like CAA and SAE-TS in single-attribute and multi-attribute control tasks.
SRS maintains high linguistic quality, including grammatical correctness and language diversity, with minimal side effects.
SRS demonstrates robustness against diverse jailbreak prompts, achieving high defense rates.
Multi-attribute control with PCA composition strategy yields the best trade-off between control effectiveness and content quality.
Sparse features enable interpretable identification of attribute-relevant dimensions through KL divergence analysis.
papers.limitation: Multi-attribute steering strategies such as PCA may not fully capture complex relationships and conflicts between attributes.
future_direction: Layer-wise or component-wise multi-attribute steering to align interventions with semantic levels.
Context-aware and personalized steering based on semantic subdomains of prompts.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) exhibit impressive capabilities in generation tasks but are prone to producing harmful, misleading, or biased content, posing significant ethical and safety concerns. To mitigate such risks, representation engineering, which steer model behavior toward desired attributes by injecting carefully designed steering vectors into LLM's representations at inference time, has emerged as a promising alternative to fine-tuning approaches. However, due to the semantically entangled nature of LLM's representation, existing representation engineering methods still suffer from several limitations: limited fine-grained controllability, content quality degradation, and conflict in multi-attribute control. To overcome these challenges, we propose Sparse Representation Steering (SRS), a novel framework that achieves fine-grained and interpretable control over LLM behavior by first disentangling internal activations into a sparse, semantically meaningful representation space, and then selectively steering relevant dimensions. Specifically, SRS leverages a pretrained Sparse Autoencoder (SAE) to transform dense, entangled activation patterns into a sparse monosemantic feature space. To identify relevant features, SRS contrasts sparse activations from positive and negative prompt pairs and measures their bidirectional KL divergence to locate dimensions most associated with the target attribute. We conduct comprehensive experiments on Gemma-2 series model across three alignment dimensions, i.e., safety, fairness, and truthfulness, to evaluate the effectiveness of SRS. Results show that SRS consistently outperforms existing steering methods, which achieves significantly improved controllability across both single and multiple attribute settings, while preserving high linguistic quality and general ability.

papers.title: Understanding Reasoning in Thinking Language Models via Steering Vectors
papers.research_question: Can reasoning behaviors in thinking language models be controlled using steering vectors?
papers.core_contribution: The paper demonstrates that reasoning behaviors in thinking LLMs are mediated by linear directions in the activation space and can be controlled using steering vectors extracted via difference of means and attribution patching.
papers.conclusion: Steering vectors provide a practical method for controlling reasoning behaviors in thinking models, opening new possibilities for fine-grained control of model behavior.
papers.key_findings:
Thinking models exhibit distinct reasoning behaviors such as backtracking, uncertainty estimation, and example testing.
These behaviors are mediated by linear directions in the model's activation space.
Steering vectors extracted via difference of means can control these behaviors, increasing or decreasing their occurrence.
The steering approach works across different model architectures within the DeepSeek-R1-Distill family.
The method provides a practical tool for modulating reasoning capabilities in thinking models.
papers.limitation:
The automated annotation process using GPT-4o has occasionally produced false positives and false negatives in identifying reasoning patterns.
The generalization of these findings to other models that have undergone reward-based RL training instead of being fine-tuned on thinking models remains an open question.
future_direction: Developing more robust annotation methods, potentially incorporating multiple models or human validation.
Extending the research to a broader range of models to understand the universality of thinking mechanisms.
papers.abstract: Recent advances in large language models (LLMs) have led to the development of thinking language models that generate extensive internal reasoning chains before producing responses. While these models achieve improved performance, controlling their reasoning processes remains challenging. This work presents a steering approach for thinking LLMs by analyzing and manipulating specific reasoning behaviors in DeepSeek-R1-Distill models. Through a systematic experiment on 500 tasks across 10 diverse categories, we identify several reasoning behaviors exhibited by thinking models, including expressing uncertainty, generating examples for hypothesis validation, and backtracking in reasoning chains. We demonstrate that these behaviors are mediated by linear directions in the model's activation space and can be controlled using steering vectors. By extracting and applying these vectors, we provide a method to modulate specific aspects of the model's reasoning process, such as its tendency to backtrack or express uncertainty. Our approach offers practical tools for steering reasoning processes in thinking models in a controlled and interpretable manner. We validate our steering method using three DeepSeek-R1-Distill models, demonstrating consistent control across different model architectures.

papers.title: On the Biology of a Large Language Model
papers.research_question: How do large language models internally perform computations, and can we reverse engineer their mechanisms using attribution graphs?
papers.core_contribution: This work applies attribution graphs to Claude 3.5 Haiku, uncovering sophisticated internal mechanisms like multi-step reasoning, planning, and metacognitive circuits, demonstrating the value of unsupervised tools for model interpretability.
papers.conclusion: Attribution graphs enable detailed reverse engineering of model internals, revealing complex strategies and advancing the field of AI interpretability.
papers.key_findings:
The model performs genuine two-hop reasoning with intermediate steps, such as representing 'Texas' when answering about the capital of the state containing Dallas.
In poetry generation, the model plans ahead by pre-selecting rhyming words before writing each line.
Multilingual circuits use a mix of language-specific and abstract, language-independent components, with more abstraction in larger models.
Entity recognition circuits distinguish known and unknown entities, influencing when the model answers or refuses, with circuit misfires causing hallucinations.
Refusal mechanisms involve harmful request features aggregated from pretraining and trigger refusal during fine-tuning.
papers.limitation:
tools provide satisfying insight for about a quarter of prompts
replacement model incompletely and imperfectly captures the original model
future_direction: Developing more effective unsupervised exploration tools for increasingly capable models
papers.abstract: How do large language models internally perform computations, and can we reverse engineer their mechanisms using attribution graphs? This work applies attribution graphs to Claude 3.5 Haiku, uncovering sophisticated internal mechanisms like multi-step reasoning, planning, and metacognitive circuits, demonstrating the value of unsupervised tools for model interpretability. Attribution graphs enable detailed reverse engineering of model internals, revealing complex strategies and advancing the field of AI interpretability.

papers.title: Probing the Representational Power of Sparse Autoencoders in Vision Models
papers.research_question: How effective are Sparse Autoencoders (SAEs) for interpreting and steering vision models, and do they provide semantically meaningful features across different vision architectures?
papers.core_contribution: SAEs extract semantically meaningful features from vision models, improve out-of-distribution generalization, and enable semantic steering in diffusion models, establishing SAEs as a valuable interpretability tool for vision.
papers.conclusion: SAE features are semantically meaningful and enhance interpretable understanding across vision encoders, multimodal LLMs, and diffusion models, highlighting SAEs as a unified interpretability tool across diverse vision architectures.
papers.key_findings:
SAE features from vision encoders improve out-of-distribution generalization compared to original embeddings.
SAE features capture hierarchical semantic structures (ontological features) in image encoders.
SAEs enable semantic steering in diffusion models by manipulating text encoder features.
SAEs reveal shared representations across vision and language modalities in LMMs.
Different SAE variants (ReLU, TopK, Gated) show similar trends in reconstruction and sparsity.
papers.limitation:
Findings on multimodal representation overlap in LMMs are preliminary and require future quantitative validation.
Steering Stable Diffusion 3.5 is more challenging due to its complex text encoding architecture.
future_direction: Quantitative validation of multimodal representation overlap in LMMs.
Systematic investigation of how visual representations evolve through LLM layers.
Future application of SAEs in vision models.
papers.abstract: Sparse Autoencoders (SAEs) have emerged as a popular tool for interpreting the hidden states of large language models (LLMs). By learning to reconstruct activations from a sparse bottleneck layer, SAEs discover interpretable features from the high-dimensional internal representations of LLMs. Despite their popularity with language models, SAEs remain understudied in the visual domain. In this work, we provide an extensive evaluation the representational power of SAEs for vision models using a broad range of image-based tasks. Our experimental results demonstrate that SAE features are semantically meaningful, improve out-of-distribution generalization, and enable controllable generation across three vision model architectures: vision embedding models, multi-modal LMMs and diffusion models. In vision embedding models, we find that learned SAE features can be used for OOD detection and provide evidence that they recover the ontological structure of the underlying model. For diffusion models, we demonstrate that SAEs enable semantic steering through text encoder manipulation and develop an automated pipeline for discovering human-interpretable attributes. Finally, we conduct exploratory experiments on multi-modal LLMs, finding evidence that SAE features reveal shared representations across vision and language modalities. Our study provides a foundation for SAE evaluation in vision models, highlighting their strong potential improving interpretability, generalization, and steerability in the visual domain.

papers.title: Protein Circuit Tracing via Cross-layer Transcoders
papers.research_question: How can we uncover the computational circuits in protein language models that underlie their predictions?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces ProtoMech, a framework using cross-layer transcoders to discover computational circuits in protein language models, achieving high performance recovery and enabling protein design.
papers.conclusion: ProtoMech establishes a principled framework for protein circuit tracing, revealing interpretable computational pathways and enabling effective protein design.
papers.key_findings:
ProtoMech recovers 82–89% of the original ESM2 performance on protein family classification and function prediction tasks.
ProtoMech identifies compact circuits using <1% of the latent space while retaining up to 79% of model accuracy.
Steering along the discovered circuits enables high-fitness protein design, outperforming baseline methods in more than 70% of cases.
The circuits correspond to known structural and functional motifs, such as binding sites and catalytic loops.
ProtoMech provides a more accurate approximation of ESM2's computation than per-layer transcoder baselines.
papers.limitation: Full replacement models, where both attention and MLP computations are replaced, lead to substantial performance degradation due to compounding reconstruction errors.
future_direction: Developing robust full replacement models remains an active area of research.
Using a tanh loss for constraining sparsity is an interesting future direction.
papers.abstract: Protein language models (pLMs) have emerged as powerful predictors of protein structure and function. However, the computational circuits underlying their predictions remain poorly understood. Recent mechanistic interpretability methods decompose pLM representations into interpretable features, but they treat each layer independently and thus fail to capture cross-layer computation, limiting their ability to approximate the full model. We introduce ProtoMech, a framework for discovering computational circuits in pLMs using cross-layer transcoders that learn sparse latent representations jointly across layers to capture the model's full computational circuitry. Applied to the pLM ESM2, ProtoMech recovers 82-89% of the original performance on protein family classification and function prediction tasks. ProtoMech then identifies compressed circuits that use <1% of the latent space while retaining up to 79% of model accuracy, revealing correspondence with structural and functional motifs, including binding, signaling, and stability. Steering along these circuits enables high-fitness protein design, surpassing baseline methods in more than 70% of cases. These results establish ProtoMech as a principled framework for protein circuit tracing.

papers.title: Evolution of Concepts in Language Model Pre-Training
papers.research_question: How do features in language models emerge and evolve internally during pre-training? What is the internal dynamics of model pre-training?
papers.core_contribution: This paper introduces a method using cross-snapshot crosscoders to track the evolution of interpretable features during language model pre-training, revealing a two-phase learning process (statistical then feature learning) and establishing causal connections between feature formation and downstream task performance.
papers.conclusion: The work demonstrates that cross-snapshot crosscoders can successfully track fine-grained feature evolution during pre-training, providing empirical evidence for a statistical-to-feature-learning phase transition and opening possibilities for detailed analysis of representation learning dynamics.
papers.key_findings:
Feature evolution follows a two-phase pattern: a statistical learning phase followed by a feature learning phase, with most features beginning to form around step 1000.
Decoder norms of crosscoder features serve as effective proxies for tracking feature strength and presence across training snapshots.
More complex features (e.g., induction, context-sensitive) tend to emerge later in training than simpler features (e.g., previous token).
Attribution-based circuit tracing shows that the formation of specific crosscoder features causally contributes to improvements on downstream tasks like subject-verb agreement.
Features undergo a universal directional shift around step 1000, after which they rotate more gradually while maintaining similarity to their post-step 1000 orientations.
papers.limitation: Crosscoders may theoretically misalign unrelated features or split shared features across snapshots, though the authors argue these are rare in practice.
papers.abstract: Language models obtain extensive capabilities through pre-training. However, the pre-training process remains a black box. In this work, we track linear interpretable feature evolution across pre-training snapshots using a sparse dictionary learning method called crosscoders. We find that most features begin to form around a specific point, while more complex patterns emerge in later training stages. Feature attribution analyses reveal causal connections between feature evolution and downstream performance. Our feature-level observations are highly consistent with previous findings on Transformer's two-stage learning process, which we term a statistical learning phase and a feature learning phase. Our work opens up the possibility to track fine-grained representation progress during language model learning dynamics.

papers.title: SAE-SSV: Supervised Steering in Sparse Representation Spaces for Reliable Control of Language Models
papers.research_question: How can we reliably control large language model behavior in open-ended generation settings by using supervised steering in sparse, interpretable representation spaces?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces a supervised steering framework (SAE-SSV) that constrains interventions to a sparse, task-relevant latent subspace identified via labeled data and sparse autoencoders, enabling more targeted control and better preservation of generation quality.
papers.conclusion: SAE-SSV enables effective LLM steering by operating in sparse, task-specific subspaces, outperforming existing methods and providing a more targeted and interpretable approach to behavior control.
papers.key_findings:
SAE-SSV consistently outperforms baseline steering methods (CAA, RePe, Top PC, ITI) in steering success rate across sentiment, truthfulness, and political polarity tasks.
